name: Gambas al Ajillo
description: Spain's most seductive tapa — prawns seared in an inferno of olive oil, garlic, and dried chile until the shells spit and sizzle, eaten straight from the clay cazuela with torn bread to drag through the garlicky oil.
ingredients: 16 raw prawns, shell-on and deveineds (400 g)
½ cup extra-virgin olive oil (100 ml)
2 dried guindilla peppers or red chiles
¼ cup dry sherry, fino or manzanilla (60 ml)
A handful of fresh flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped
steps: Pour the olive oil into a cazuela, heavy skillet, or cast-iron pan. Set over the highest heat your stove allows. Wait patiently — the oil needs to be genuinely ripping hot, shimmering and almost smoking, before anything else goes in. A thermometer reads around 180 C (356 F). This extreme heat is not optional: it's what causes the prawns to sear rather than steam, and the garlic to perfume rather than burn.

Add the sliced garlic and whole dried chiles to the blazing oil in one confident movement. They will spit and sizzle violently — this is correct. Swirl the pan or use a wooden spoon to keep the garlic in constant motion. The window is narrow: you want the garlic golden at the edges, just slightly translucent at the center, with a nutty fragrance rising from the pan. About 30–45 seconds total.

Season the prawns lightly with salt, then add them to the pan in a single layer. Do not crowd — if your pan is small, work in two batches. The prawns must make contact with the hot oil, not with each other. Let them sear undisturbed for 60–90 seconds until the underside has turned coral-pink and opaque halfway up the flesh. The shells should be starting to char at the edges. Then flip each prawn.

Flip all prawns, then immediately pour in the dry sherry. The pan will roar and steam dramatically. The alcohol will flare briefly if you are on a gas stove — this is fine. Swirl the pan to dissolve the caramelized fond from the bottom and coat the prawns. Cook for 30 seconds more until the prawns are fully pink and the sherry has reduced to a glossy emulsion in the oil.

Off the heat, squeeze the lemon juice directly over the prawns and scatter the chopped parsley. Swirl the pan once more to combine. The acid from the lemon will cut through the richness of the oil and lift the entire dish. Transfer immediately to a warmed cazuela or serve directly from the pan — gambas al ajillo must arrive at the table still sizzling, with the garlicky oil pooled at the bottom for bread.

name: Potato Gnocchi
description: Cloud-light pillow-dumplings made from still-warm baked potato, just enough flour, and a single egg — the Italian grandmother's paradox: the less you work the dough, the better the gnocchi. One extra gram of flour is the difference between a dumpling and a torpedo.
ingredients: 5 russet or Yukon Gold potatoes, floury variety (1000 g)
1⅓ cups all-purpose flour, plus extra for bench (200 g)
⅓ cup parmigiano-Reggiano, grated; optional finish (30 g)
2½ tablespoons unsalted butter, for pan sauce (40 g)
steps: Preheat oven to 200 C (400 F). Scrub potatoes, prick all over with a fork, and place directly on the oven rack (not wrapped in foil — you want moisture to escape). Bake for 55–70 minutes until completely tender through the center when pierced with a skewer and the skin is papery and tight. Do not boil the potatoes — boiling adds water, which demands more flour, which makes heavy gnocchi.

While potatoes are still steaming hot, halve them and scoop the flesh directly through a ricer or food mill onto a clean board or baking sheet. Spread the riced potato in a thin layer and let the steam escape for 3–4 minutes. Do not mash with a masher — it crushes the cells and creates a gluey paste. Cool just until you can handle it, but no more.

Make a well in the riced potato. Add the beaten egg and salt into the well. Scatter the flour over the top. Using a bench scraper or your fingertips, cut and fold the mixture together — do not knead. Work until just combined: a shaggy dough forms and no dry flour remains. The moment you see a cohesive mass, stop. Over-working develops gluten and makes gnocchi tough.

Flour your work surface lightly. Tear off a golf-ball portion of dough and roll it into a rope about 1.5 cm in diameter, applying even pressure from the center outward. Cut the rope into 2 cm pillows with a bench scraper. Optional: roll each piece over a fork or gnocchi board, pressing gently with your thumb to create ridges that hold sauce. Place on a lightly floured baking sheet in a single layer.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a vigorous boil. Cook gnocchi in batches of 20–25 pieces. They are done the moment they bob to the surface and have stayed there for 30 seconds — no longer. Remove with a slotted spoon directly into a waiting skillet of browned butter over medium heat. Toss to coat and finish in the butter for 60 seconds until lightly golden.

name: Gnocchi al Burro e Salvia
description: Potato gnocchi made right have the texture of clouds condensed into something you can hold — impossibly light, barely structured, yielding at the touch of a fork. Brown the butter to hazelnut, fry sage leaves until they shatter, and the whole thing becomes northern Italian winter in a bowl.
ingredients: 2½ floury potatoes, such as Russet or King Edwards, about 700g before baking (500 g)
¾ cup 00 flour, plus more for the bench (130 g)
⅓ cup unsalted butter, European-style, 84% fat (80 g)
A small handful of fresh sage leaves, 8-10 large
½ cup parmigiano Reggiano, finely grated, to finish (40 g)
steps: Bake the unpeeled potatoes at 200°C (400°F) directly on the oven rack until completely tender — a skewer inserted meets no resistance, about 50 to 60 minutes. Baking, not boiling, is critical: boiling adds water to the potato, which forces you to add more flour for structure, and more flour means heavier gnocchi. While still steaming hot, halve the potatoes, scoop the flesh, and pass immediately through a potato ricer or fine-mesh drum sieve onto a clean, lightly floured surface. Spread the riced potato out and let the steam escape for 3 minutes.

Make a well in the centre of the riced potato. Add the egg yolk, salt, and about 100g of the flour. Using a bench scraper or your fingertips, work the flour into the potato with a cutting and folding motion — not kneading. Add more flour a tablespoon at a time only as needed. The dough is ready the moment it just comes together and no longer sticks to your hands. Overworking develops gluten and makes the gnocchi tough — the dough should feel pillowy and barely cohesive, almost impossibly soft.

Divide the dough into 6 portions. On a lightly floured surface, roll each portion into a rope about 1.5cm in diameter — roll from the centre outward with flat palms, applying even pressure. Cut into 2cm pieces with a bench scraper or sharp knife. For the classic ridged gnocchi, roll each piece down the back of a fork with your thumb, creating a slight curl and ridges that grip the sauce. Place on a floured baking sheet in a single layer. Cook within 30 minutes or freeze immediately.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil. Meanwhile, in a wide skillet, melt the butter over medium heat and continue cooking until the milk solids turn golden brown and the butter smells of toasted hazelnuts, about 3 to 4 minutes. Add sage leaves and fry until crisp and translucent, 30 to 45 seconds. Lower the heat to minimum. Drop gnocchi into boiling water in a single batch — they are ready about 30 seconds after they float to the surface. Remove with a spider directly into the brown butter pan, adding a splash of pasta water. Toss gently over medium heat for 30 seconds to coat, then serve immediately with grated Parmesan.

name: Greek Baked Sea Bass (Lavraki Plaki)
description: A whole sea bass laid on a bed of tomatoes, onions, and potatoes, drowned in olive oil and white wine, and baked low and slow until everything is silky and the fish falls from the bone at a glance.
ingredients: 1100 g whole sea bass, 1–1.2kg, cleaned; lavraki
½ cup extra-virgin olive oil (100 ml)
1 white onion, sliced into rings (200 g)
1½ waxy potatoes, peeled and sliced 5mm (300 g)
½ cup dry white wine (100 ml)
A handful of fresh flat-leaf parsley (20 g)
1¾ teaspoons fine sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
steps: Preheat the oven to 180°C (350°F). In a large roasting dish or oven-safe skillet, layer the potato slices across the bottom. Add the onion rings, tomato slices, and garlic over the top. Season generously with salt and pepper. Pour 60ml of olive oil and the white wine over the vegetables. Add the thyme sprigs. Bake for 25 minutes until the potatoes have begun to soften and the tomatoes are beginning to collapse. The preliminary bake ensures the potatoes are cooked through — they need more time than the fish.

Score the fish 3 times on each side. Season inside and out with salt and pepper. Stuff the cavity with parsley, lemon rounds, and a drizzle of olive oil. Lay the fish on top of the partially cooked vegetable bed. Drizzle the remaining olive oil over the fish. Arrange the remaining lemon rounds on top. Return to the oven for 30–35 minutes until the fish is cooked through. Spoon the pan juices over the fish twice during cooking.

Bring the entire roasting dish to the table — this is the way plaki is served. Scatter fresh parsley over the top. Each person takes a portion of fish and a spoonful of the vegetables and fragrant pan juices beneath. Serve with crusty bread to mop up the juices.

name: Gigantes Plaki
description: Enormous white butter beans baked low and slow in a rich tomato sauce with olive oil, celery, and sweet onion until their skins split and their interiors become creamy and yielding — the sauce reducing to a thick, tomatoey glaze that the beans absorb like sponges.
ingredients: 2 cups dried gigantes beans, soaked overnight; giant white beans (400 g)
A tin of crushed canned tomatoes (400 g)
⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil (80 ml)
½ teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground
¾ cup water or vegetable stock (200 ml)
steps: Drain the soaked beans and rinse well. Cover with fresh cold water in a large pot by at least 5 cm. Bring to a boil, skim off any white foam that rises in the first 5 minutes. Reduce to a vigorous simmer and cook for 45 to 60 minutes until the beans are tender but still slightly firm at the center — they will finish in the oven. Drain and reserve.

Preheat oven to 180 C (350 F). In a large, wide oven-safe pan or skillet, heat half the olive oil over medium heat. Add onion, garlic, and celery. Cook, stirring, for 12 to 15 minutes until everything is very soft, sweet-smelling, and just beginning to turn golden at the edges. Do not rush this step.

Add the tomato paste to the soffritto and stir for 2 minutes until it darkens from bright red to rust-brown (this is pinçage — it mellows the acidity). Add the crushed tomatoes, sugar, salt, pepper, and water or stock. Stir to combine. Simmer for 10 minutes until slightly thickened.

Gently fold the parboiled beans into the tomato sauce in the pan. Drizzle the remaining olive oil over the top. Transfer to the preheated oven uncovered. Bake for 50 to 60 minutes, turning the beans once at the halfway point, until the sauce is thick and jammy and the top layer of beans has formed a slightly caramelized, darkened crust. Scatter fresh parsley over the top just before serving.

name: Grilled Asparagus with Lemon and Parmesan
description: Thick asparagus spears rolled in olive oil and grilled at high heat until the tips blister to a charred, crispy fringe and the stalks take on sweet, smoky char while remaining tender enough to snap cleanly — finished with bright lemon and nutty shaved parmesan.
ingredients: 2 bunches of thick asparagus spears, woody ends snapped off (500 g)
3 tablespoons lemon, zest and juice (50 g)
steps: Bend each asparagus spear gently near the base — it will snap naturally at the point where woody fibre gives way to tender stalk. Discard the woody ends (or use for stock). Toss the spears in olive oil until each one glistens. Season with salt. The asparagus must be dry before you add oil — any water will steam the grill grate and the spears will steam rather than char.

Place spears perpendicular to the grill grates on a very hot grill or ridged cast-iron grill pan (preheated to screaming hot). Grill without moving for 2–3 minutes until char marks develop, then roll 90 degrees and grill a further 2 minutes. The asparagus should show distinct char at the grill marks and the tips should be frizzled and blistered. Total cook time: 4–6 minutes for thick spears.

Arrange the hot spears on a serving plate. Squeeze lemon juice generously over all of them and zest the lemon directly over the top. Drape shaved parmesan ribbons over the spears while still hot so they soften slightly. Crack fresh black pepper over the top. The acid and salt of the lemon must be applied while the asparagus is still hot enough to absorb it.

name: Grilled Whole Branzino
description: A whole European sea bass seasoned simply with olive oil, lemon, and herbs, grilled over fierce heat until the skin blisters and shatters and the sweet flesh inside steams in its own juices — Mediterranean cooking at its most honest and dramatic.
ingredients: 2 whole branzinos, cleaned and scaled, about 500g each; European sea bass
¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil (60 ml)
2 lemon, half for juice, half sliced thins
steps: Using a sharp knife, make 3 diagonal cuts through the skin and flesh on each side of each fish — angled at 45 degrees toward the head, about 1 cm deep and 4 cm long, evenly spaced from the shoulder to the tail. These scores serve two purposes: they allow heat to penetrate the thickest parts of the fish more evenly, and they give the seasoning and cavity aromatics a path into the flesh. Pat the fish completely dry inside and out with paper towels — a dry fish grills, a wet fish steams.

Season the cavity of each fish generously with salt and a grind of pepper. Stuff each cavity with crushed garlic, thyme sprigs, a rosemary sprig, a few parsley sprigs, and 2–3 thin lemon slices. The herbs and lemon will perfume the fish from the inside as it cooks. Season the exterior — including into the score cuts — with salt, pepper, and a generous drizzle of olive oil. Use your hands to coat the entire outside surface, making sure oil reaches into every score.

Preheat a charcoal grill to high heat, or a gas grill to maximum (you need at least 280°C over the grate). Clean and oil the grate well — a clean, hot, oiled grate is the difference between fish that lifts off beautifully and fish that tears. Lay the fish on the grate at a 45-degree angle to the bars. Do not move the fish for 5–7 minutes. You will know it is ready to flip when the fish releases from the grate without sticking. Flip once using two wide spatulas, and cook the second side for 4–5 minutes.

Transfer the grilled fish to a warm platter and rest for 3 minutes before serving. This brief rest allows the residual heat to finish the very centre of the fish and allows the juices in the cavity to redistribute. Squeeze fresh lemon generously over the top — the acid brightens the smoky richness of the grilled skin. Present the fish whole at the table, and use a wide spatula and fork to fillet it tableside: lift the top fillet along the spine, then remove the backbone to reveal the bottom fillet.

name: Gyoza — Pan-Fried Pork & Cabbage Dumplings
description: Thin-skinned crescents of pork and cabbage that are steamed and then seared in a single unbroken maneuver, producing a crisp caramelized bottom and a taut, translucent top. They release from the pan in one dramatic sheet.
ingredients: 1¾ cups Napa cabbage, finely minced (150 g)
30 gyoza wrappers, round, store-bought or homemade
2 handfuls of garlic chives, thinly sliced; nira (30 g)
1½ tablespoons neutral oil for frying, rice bran (20 ml)
⅓ cup water, for steam-frying (80 ml)
steps: Mince the napa cabbage very finely — each piece no larger than a sesame seed. Toss with the full measure of salt in a large bowl and massage it briefly. Let stand 10 minutes. The salt will pull an astonishing volume of water from the cabbage — you want to remove it, not cook with it. After 10 minutes, gather the cabbage in a clean cloth or your fist and squeeze with real force, twisting until almost no liquid drips. Do not skip this step. Wet cabbage will steam the dumpling from the inside during frying, preventing the bottom from crisping and causing the filling to become watery and loose. The squeezed cabbage should feel almost dry, reduced to roughly one-third its original volume.

Combine the squeezed cabbage with the ground pork, garlic paste, grated ginger, garlic chives, soy sauce, sesame oil, and white pepper in a large bowl. Mix using your hand (not a spoon) in one direction only — always clockwise or always counter-clockwise. This directional mixing aligns the proteins and builds a light binding structure that helps the filling stay cohesive when bitten. Mix for 90 seconds until the filling feels slightly sticky and holds its shape when pinched. Do not overwork or the pork fat will break and the filling will be greasy. Taste the raw filling — Japanese cooks taste it raw to calibrate seasoning. It should taste assertively seasoned, because the wrapper will dilute the flavors. Adjust soy sauce if needed.

Work with one wrapper at a time, keeping the others under a damp cloth. Place a wrapper on your non-dominant palm. Spoon 10–12 g of filling (roughly a leveled teaspoon) into the center — do not overfill. Dip your finger in water and wet the entire rim of the wrapper. Fold the wrapper in half to form a half-moon, pinching the center point closed with thumb and forefinger. Now pleat only the front side: starting from the center, push the front skin into three or four small folds toward the right, then repeat to the left. The back skin should remain smooth — this asymmetry is what creates the characteristic crescent and ensures the gyoza stands upright. Press each pleat firmly against the smooth back to seal. Place sealed side down on a parchment-lined tray. The base should be flat enough to sit without wobbling.

Heat a flat-bottomed non-stick or carbon-steel skillet over medium-high until a drop of water skips and evaporates instantly. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat. Working quickly, arrange the gyoza flat-side down in tight concentric rows or a single layer — they can touch. Fry undisturbed for 90 seconds until the bottoms are pale golden. Now pour in the water all at once: it will scream and steam violently. Immediately cover with a tight-fitting lid. The steam will cook the tops and fill the interior. Steam-fry 5–6 minutes until the water has entirely evaporated — you will hear the sizzle change from a wet hiss to a dry crackle. Remove the lid and fry 1–2 more minutes until the bottoms are deep amber and the skin pulls slightly away from the pan. Drizzle a few drops of sesame oil around the edge if desired. Invert onto a plate in one motion so the golden bases face up.

name: Haricots Verts Amandine
description: Tender-crisp French green beans blanched to vivid green and finished in foamy browned butter scattered with toasted slivered almonds — the essence of classical French elegance.
ingredients: 4 cups haricots verts, stem ends trimmed, French green beans (400 g)
½ teaspoon freshly ground white pepper
steps: Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Season it with salt until it tastes like mild sea water — about 15 g salt per litre. Drop the haricots verts in and cook uncovered for exactly 2–3 minutes: the goal is crisp-tender, never soft. Have a large bowl of ice water ready. Drain the beans and immediately plunge them into the ice bath.

In a wide sauté pan over medium heat, melt the butter and add the slivered almonds simultaneously. Swirl the pan frequently. The butter will foam, then the foam will subside as water evaporates. Watch carefully — the milk solids will begin to color to a toasty brown while the almonds toast alongside them. The moment the butter smells of hazelnuts and the almonds are golden, remove from heat.

Add the drained and thoroughly dried beans to the pan with the beurre noisette and almonds. Toss over medium-low heat for 1 minute until the beans are coated and reheated. Squeeze the lemon juice directly over the pan and toss once more. Season with white pepper and taste for salt. Serve immediately on a warmed plate.

name: Harira
description: Morocco's beloved tomato-lentil-chickpea soup eaten to break the Ramadan fast — lamb, lentils, and chickpeas simmered with cinnamon, ginger, and coriander, thickened with a flour-tomato paste called tedouira and brightened with preserved lemon.
ingredients: 500 g lamb shoulder, cut into 2cm cubes
¾ cup green or brown lentils, rinsed (150 g)
1¼ cups cooked chickpeas, or canned, drained (200 g)
3 ripe tomatoes, grated or canned crushed (400 g)
2 handfuls of fresh coriander, chopped; stems and leaves separated (30 g)
A handful of flat-leaf parsley, chopped (20 g)
2 tablespoons preserved lemon rind, white pith removed, minced (20 g)
3 tablespoons all-purpose flour, for tedouira (30 g)
½ cup cold water, for tedouira, whisked with flour (120 g)
6½ cups water or light lamb stock (1500 g)
steps: Set a large, heavy pot (at least 5 liters) over medium-high heat and add the olive oil. When the oil shimmers, add the lamb cubes in a single layer — do not crowd or the meat will steam rather than sear. Brown on two or three sides, about 3 minutes per side, developing a deep mahogany crust. Remove the browned lamb to a plate. In the same pot, reduce heat to medium and add the diced onion with a pinch of salt. Cook, scraping up the fond, for 5–7 minutes until the onion is soft and translucent. Add the coriander stems (reserve the leaves), cinnamon, ginger, turmeric, and black pepper directly to the onion. Stir and fry the spices for 60–90 seconds until they smell intensely fragrant and have dried out any remaining onion moisture. Return the seared lamb to the pot and stir to coat.

Pour the grated or crushed tomatoes over the spiced lamb and stir to combine, scraping up any fond from the base of the pot. Add the rinsed lentils and pour in the water or lamb stock. Bring to a vigorous boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady, gentle simmer — lid slightly ajar. Skim any grey foam that rises in the first ten minutes; this is coagulated blood protein from the lamb and you want it off the surface for a clean broth. Simmer for 45–50 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lentils have completely softened and begun to dissolve into the broth and the lamb is fully tender and yielding. The soup should have reduced and thickened slightly from the lentil starch.

In a small bowl, whisk the all-purpose flour with the cold water until completely smooth and lump-free — this is the tedouira, harira's traditional thickener and one of the things that makes it distinctly Moroccan rather than a generic lentil soup. Cold water is essential; hot water begins cooking the starch and creates lumps. Whisk vigorously, starting from the center and working outward, and tip the bowl to check the corners where dry flour hides. Let it stand 2 minutes, then whisk again — any remaining lumps will show up. A clean, perfectly smooth milky-white slurry is what you're after.

Add the chickpeas to the simmering soup and stir to incorporate. While the soup is at a steady simmer (not boiling), pour in the tedouira in a slow, steady stream while stirring constantly with a long spoon in wide circles. Pour slowly and stir continuously — this is the motion that prevents lumps. The soup will thicken noticeably within 2–3 minutes as the flour starch cooks out. Keep it at a gentle simmer for 5 more minutes to cook the flour completely; raw flour will make the soup taste starchy rather than silky. In the final minute, stir in the minced preserved lemon rind, chopped coriander leaves, and flat-leaf parsley. Taste and adjust salt. Serve immediately in deep bowls — harira waits for no one.

name: Huevos Rancheros
description: Fried eggs settled onto a warm corn tortilla and smothered in a bracing roasted salsa roja — a Mexican ranch breakfast of pure contrasts: crunchy tortilla, runny yolk, smoky heat.
ingredients: 2 dried guajillo or ancho chilies, stemmed, seeded
Half a medium white onion, halved
2 tablespoons cotija cheese or queso fresco, crumbled
steps: Heat a dry comal, cast-iron skillet, or flat griddle over high heat until very hot. Place the tomatoes, halved onion, and unpeeled garlic directly on the dry surface. Char them, turning occasionally, until the tomato skins blister and blacken in patches, the onion surfaces are dark brown, and the garlic is soft and fragrant — about 10 minutes total. Meanwhile, toast the dried chilies in the same dry pan for 30 seconds per side until they puff slightly and smell toasty but not burnt, then soak them in enough boiling water to cover for 10 minutes until pliable.

Peel the garlic. Add the charred tomatoes (with their juices), peeled garlic, browned onion pieces, and drained softened chilies to a blender. Blend until smooth — or leave slightly rough if you prefer a rustic texture. Season with salt. In a saucepan, heat one tablespoon of oil until shimmering, then pour the blended salsa in all at once — it will spit and splatter dramatically for 30 seconds. Fry the salsa, stirring, for 3–4 minutes until it darkens by a shade and the raw onion-garlic edge cooks out. The brief fry transforms blended ingredients into a cohesive sauce.

In a separate skillet, heat the remaining oil over medium-high heat. Pass each tortilla through the oil for 20–30 seconds per side — just long enough to warm through and pick up a few golden spots, but not enough to make them fully rigid. They should be pliable enough to fold but have a light crunch at the rim. Drain briefly on paper towels. Transfer to a warmed plate.

In the same skillet (or another), heat a film of oil over medium heat. Crack the eggs in carefully, keeping yolks intact. Fry sunny-side up: spoon hot oil over the whites to set the top edge, or cover with a lid for 1 minute to steam-set the whites without flipping. The whites should be fully set and opaque, with the yolk still completely liquid and bright orange-gold. Season with a pinch of salt.

Place the warm tortilla(s) on a plate. Slide the fried egg on top. Ladle the warm salsa generously over the egg white, leaving the yolk uncovered or just barely brushed so it remains visible and bright. Scatter crumbled cotija and fresh cilantro over the top. Serve with lime wedges on the side. Everything should arrive at the table hot — this is an assembly job that takes 30 seconds.

name: Italian Acqua Pazza
description: Fish poached in 'crazy water' — a bubbling broth of cherry tomatoes, white wine, and olive oil that drives itself to a boil in the pan, perfuming the fish with the sea breeze of the southern Italian coast.
ingredients: 1000 g whole fish, cleaned; sea bream, snapper, or sea bass
⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil (80 ml)
⅔ cup dry white wine (150 ml)
¾ cup water or light fish stock (200 ml)
A handful of fresh flat-leaf parsley (20 g)
¾ teaspoon dried peperoncino, red chili flakes
2 tablespoons good-quality caper berries or capers (20 g)
steps: In a wide, lidded skillet or shallow casserole, warm the olive oil over medium heat. Add the bruised garlic and peperoncino and cook gently for 1 minute until fragrant. Add the cherry tomatoes cut-side down and cook for 3 minutes until they begin to blister and collapse. Add the white wine and let it bubble for 1 minute. Add the water or fish stock and the capers. Season with salt. Bring to a vigorous simmer.

Score the fish 3 times on each side. Season inside and out. Lower the fish into the simmering broth. Cover the pan and cook over medium heat for 8–10 minutes per 500g of fish. Spoon the broth over the fish every 3 minutes. The fish is cooked when the score cuts have opened and the eye of the fish has turned white and opaque — this is the Neapolitan fisherman's traditional indicator of doneness.

Scatter torn fresh parsley leaves over the fish and drizzle a final thread of raw olive oil over the broth. Serve directly from the pan at the table. Provide good crusty bread for the broth — the acqua pazza (crazy water) is the real treasure: a light, herb-bright, tomato-scented essence that should be drunk from the bowl at the end.

name: Kinpira Gobo (Braised Burdock and Carrot)
description: Julienned burdock root and carrot sautéed in sesame oil and simmered in a sweet soy glaze until each strand is tender but still has the faintest, satisfying resistance — a Japanese comfort side that rewards patience with the knife.
ingredients: 200 g burdock root, scrubbed, julienned; gobo
1½ tablespoons soy sauce, tamari for gluten-free (25 ml)
1½ tablespoons sake, or dry sherry (20 ml)
½ teaspoon dried red chili flakes, togarashi, optional
steps: Scrub the burdock root with a stiff brush under cold water — do not peel, the skin carries earthiness and nutrition. Cut into 5cm matchsticks (julienne), approximately 3–4mm square. As you cut, immediately transfer to a bowl of cold water with a splash of rice vinegar or lemon juice to prevent oxidation. Burdock discolors dramatically and quickly when exposed to air — within minutes it will turn from cream to dark brown. Drain and pat dry just before cooking.

Heat the sesame oil in a wok or medium skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chili flakes and stir for 10 seconds until fragrant. Add the drained, dried burdock matchsticks and the julienned carrot. Stir-fry over high heat for 3–4 minutes, tossing regularly, until the vegetables are beginning to pick up color and the burdock has softened slightly at the surface but is still firm at the center. The sesame oil should smell nutty and toasty.

Add the sake first — it will sizzle and reduce in 30 seconds. Add the mirin and soy sauce. Reduce heat to medium. Toss the vegetables in the glaze, then cook, stirring regularly, for 4–5 minutes until the liquid has reduced to a thin, glossy glaze that coats every strand. The burdock should be tender but with a slight, distinctive resistance at the core — kinpira is never soft. Taste for seasoning — it should be sweet, salty, and faintly earthy.

Transfer to a small serving dish or bowls. Scatter toasted sesame seeds generously over the top. Serve at room temperature as a banchan alongside rice. Kinpira gobo keeps refrigerated for 3–4 days and actually improves overnight as the glaze penetrates deeper into the burdock.

name: Japanese Onigiri
description: Warm seasoned rice compressed into a firm triangle, its salty nori exterior crackling at the first bite to reveal a savory filling hidden at the center — Japan's perfect portable meal.
ingredients: 1½ cups Japanese short-grain rice, sushi rice (300 g)
1¼ teaspoons fine sea salt, for hands and rice
40 g umeboshi or tuna mayo, pickled plum
1 teaspoon soy sauce, for wet hands, optional
steps: Rinse the rice until the water runs nearly clear (5–6 rinses). Drain and let the rice sit dry in the pot for 10 minutes — this pre-resting firms the exterior. Add the measured water, cover tightly, and bring to a boil over high heat. As soon as you hear the boiling, reduce to the absolute lowest simmer and cook for 12 minutes. Remove from heat without lifting the lid and steam for 10 minutes. The rice is ready when you open the lid to a puff of steam with no visible water at the surface.

While the rice is still warm, turn it into a large flat bowl using a rice paddle. Sprinkle the salt evenly over the surface. Fold the rice using a cutting-and-folding motion (not stirring) to distribute the salt without crushing the grains. Fan or let cool to a temperature where you can comfortably handle it — just above body temperature, around 40°C.

Wet both palms with cold water and rub with a generous pinch of salt — this prevents sticking and adds flavor to the exterior. Take about 120g of warm rice and form a loose ball in one palm. Press a shallow indentation in the center and place your filling (umeboshi, tuna mayo, or salmon flakes) inside. Close the rice around the filling. Cup both hands into a V-shape and press firmly from the sides while rotating, forming a compact triangle with three flat faces and three ridges. Wrap the base with a strip of nori. Repeat for remaining rice and fillings.

name: Japanese Salmon Teriyaki
description: Thick salmon fillets lacquered in a four-ingredient teriyaki glaze until the skin crackles and the glaze turns to a mahogany, bittersweet varnish that shatters at the fork.
ingredients: 3 tablespoons soy sauce, tamari for gluten-free
1 tablespoon neutral oil, sunflower or rice bran
steps: Combine the soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small saucepan. Bring to a boil over medium heat and stir to dissolve the sugar. Simmer for 3–4 minutes until reduced by one-third and the glaze coats the back of a spoon with a thin sheen. Remove from heat. The glaze thickens further as it cools.

Pat the salmon fillets completely dry with kitchen paper — any moisture creates steam and prevents a crust. Score the skin 3 times diagonally to prevent curling. Heat the oil in a non-stick or cast-iron pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Place the salmon skin-side down and press firmly with a spatula for 10 seconds to prevent curling. Cook skin-side down for 4 minutes until the skin is deeply golden and crisp and the flesh has turned opaque 2/3 of the way up the sides. Flip once.

After flipping, cook the flesh side for 1 minute. Reduce heat to low. Pour the teriyaki glaze over and around the salmon. As it bubbles, spoon it over the top of the fillets repeatedly for 1–2 minutes. The glaze will reduce and lacquer the salmon in a shiny, mahogany coating. Remove from heat and spoon any remaining glaze over the top. Scatter green onion and sesame seeds. Rest 1 minute before serving.

name: Japanese Tonkatsu
description: A thick pork loin cutlet, encased in a shatteringly crisp panko shell that shatters at the knife — the contrast between crackling crust and juicy, barely-pink interior is tonkatsu's entire philosophy.
ingredients: 2 pork loin chops, bone-in or boneless, 2cm thicks (400 g)
800 ml neutral oil for deep frying, vegetable/canola
¾ teaspoon salt and white pepper
steps: Using a sharp knife, score the fat cap of each cutlet at 1cm intervals — this prevents the cutlet from curling in the oil. If using thick loin chops, use a meat mallet or rolling pin to pound to an even 1.5–2cm thickness between two sheets of plastic wrap. Season both sides generously with salt and white pepper. Let the cutlets rest at room temperature for 15 minutes — a cold cutlet will drop the oil temperature and result in greasy, not crisp, breading.

Set up a three-stage breading station: flour in a shallow dish, beaten egg in a second, panko in a third. Dredge each cutlet in flour, shaking off every trace of excess — too much flour makes a gluey paste under the egg. Dip in egg, letting the excess drip off, then press firmly into the panko on both sides, gently pressing the crumbs in with your palm to ensure adhesion. The coating should be thick and even, not patchy.

Heat the oil in a heavy pot or wok to 170°C (340°F). Test with a panko crumb — it should sink, immediately sizzle, and rise to the surface within 3 seconds. Lower the cutlet in slowly, away from you, and fry for 3 minutes per side without touching. At 170°C the crust sets before the interior overcooks. Raise the temperature to 180°C (355°F) for the final 30 seconds to flash-crisp the exterior to a deep golden color. Drain on a wire rack — not paper towels, which trap steam and soften the crust.

Using a sharp knife, slice the tonkatsu crosswise into 2cm strips — the goal is to preserve the crust while revealing the interior. Serve immediately with tonkatsu sauce drizzled over or alongside, finely shredded fresh cabbage, and steamed Japanese short-grain rice. The crust will begin to soften within 10 minutes, so timing is essential.

name: Japchae
description: Silky sweet potato glass noodles tossed with julienned vegetables and soy-marinated beef, glinting under a lacquer of sesame oil and sugar — soft, chewy, and deeply savory with every forkful. Each component is cooked separately and married at the last moment so nothing loses its color or texture.
ingredients: 200 g dangmyeon, sweet potato glass noodles
150 g beef sirloin or ribeye, julienned
½ bunch of spinach, blanched and squeezed (100 g)
¼ red bell pepper, julienned (60 g)
2 tablespoons neutral oil, grapeseed or canola (30 ml)
steps: Julienne the beef into strips roughly 5 cm long and 3 mm thick, cutting against the grain. Combine 2 tablespoons of soy sauce, 1 tablespoon of sugar, 1 tablespoon of sesame oil, and all of the minced garlic in a bowl. Add the beef, toss thoroughly so every strip is coated, and let it sit at room temperature while you prep the other components — at least 15 minutes. The sugar draws out the beef's surface moisture and allows rapid caramelization in the pan. Do not salt additionally; the soy carries all the salinity the beef needs. The strips should smell deeply savory and faintly sweet, with the garlic softening and becoming aromatic as it sits.

Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Drop the dangmyeon noodles in without breaking them — they will soften and uncurl on their own. Cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent clumping. Taste a noodle: it should be fully translucent all the way through with a pleasantly chewy resistance — not gummy in the center, not mushy. Drain immediately and rinse under cold running water to stop cooking and remove excess starch. Shake the colander hard. While still warm, toss the noodles with 1 tablespoon of soy sauce and 1 teaspoon of sesame oil to season them and prevent them from sticking together. Use kitchen scissors to snip the noodles two or three times — this makes them far easier to toss and eat without losing their essential chew.

Work each vegetable separately — this is the labor of japchae and the source of its beauty. Heat a wok or wide skillet over high heat until it just begins to smoke. Add a teaspoon of neutral oil and stir-fry the carrot julienne for 90 seconds with a pinch of salt; it should still have a slight bite. Remove to a plate. Repeat with the bell pepper (60 seconds — it should stay vivid red), then the shiitake mushrooms (2 minutes, until their edges begin to brown and they smell deeply woody). For the spinach, blanch briefly in salted boiling water, drain, squeeze hard until almost dry, toss with a few drops of sesame oil and a pinch of salt. Cook the eggs as a thin jidan: beat yolks and whites separately if precision matters, cook as two thin omelets, let cool, slice into 5 cm strips. Each vegetable cooked alone retains its individual color, aroma, and texture — cooking them together muds both flavor and appearance.

Heat the wok over the highest flame your stove allows until it's visibly shimmering and beginning to smoke. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Spread the marinated beef in a single layer — do not crowd the pan or the meat will steam rather than sear. Cook undisturbed for 60–90 seconds until the bottom develops a dark caramelized crust from the sugar in the marinade. Toss and cook for another 30 seconds. The beef should be just cooked through — in a dish like japchae it should be tender, not stiff. The marinade sugar will char slightly in places, adding a pleasant bitterness that balances the sweetness of the sauce. Work in two batches if the pan is full; a crowded pan steams and the glaze turns into a puddle.

In the largest bowl or the wok itself, combine the seasoned noodles, all the cooked vegetables, and the beef. Drizzle over the remaining soy sauce, sugar, and sesame oil — taste as you go; japchae is meant to be distinctly sweet-savory, so be bold with both the sugar and the soy. Toss everything together gently but thoroughly with tongs or clean hands, lifting from the bottom to distribute everything evenly without breaking the noodles. Taste repeatedly and adjust: more sugar if it lacks warmth, more soy if it's flat, more sesame oil for richness and aroma. Transfer to a serving platter and arrange the egg jidan strips over the top. Scatter sesame seeds liberally. Japchae is excellent at room temperature and actually improves after resting 20 minutes — the noodles absorb the sauce and the flavors marry.

name: Party Jollof Rice
description: West Africa's most celebrated dish — long-grain rice cooked directly in a vivid tomato, pepper, and scotch bonnet base until each grain is stained deep red and infused with the smoky, irreplaceable flavor of the party pot.
ingredients: A tin of canned whole peeled tomatoes (400 g)
A knob of fresh ginger, peeled, roughly chopped
2 cups chicken or vegetable stock (500 ml)
¼ cup neutral oil, groundnut or sunflower (60 ml)
steps: Combine the canned tomatoes, red bell peppers, scotch bonnet, half the onion, garlic, and ginger in a blender. Blitz until completely smooth with no visible chunks — you want a liquid slurry, not a chunky salsa. The color will be a vivid brick-orange at this stage. Set aside; the puree will release a lot of steam when it hits the hot oil, so have the pot ready before you blend.

Heat the oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the remaining sliced onion and fry for 4 minutes until softened and translucent. Add the tomato paste and fry, stirring constantly, for 3 minutes until it darkens to a deep rust-red. Pour in the blended tomato-pepper purée — stand back, it will splutter dramatically. Stir in bay leaves, curry powder, thyme, and salt. Cook uncovered on medium heat, stirring every 3-4 minutes, for 20-25 minutes total, until the paste has reduced by roughly half, darkened to a deep brick-red, and the oil has separated and floats visibly on top.

Pour the stock into the reduced paste and stir vigorously to incorporate, scraping any caramelized bits from the bottom of the pot. Taste the liquid — it should be pleasantly seasoned, slightly more salty than you want the finished rice, since the rice will absorb and dilute the seasoning. Adjust salt now. Bring to a rolling boil.

Rinse the parboiled rice in cold water until the water runs mostly clear, then drain thoroughly. Add the rinsed rice to the boiling tomato base and stir once — just one firm stir to distribute the rice evenly and make sure no grains are floating above the liquid level. Add the butter in small pieces over the top. Do not stir again. Place the lid on the pot, reduce the heat to its absolute lowest setting, and cook for 30 minutes undisturbed.

After 30 minutes, lift the lid quickly and look for steam holes — small craters on the surface of the rice where steam has tunneled up through the grains. These signal that the rice is cooked through. Using a long spoon, gently scrape the bottom of the pot: you should find the 'party crust' (conkon in Nigerian), a thin layer of smoky, slightly charred rice stuck to the pot floor. Fold this crust up through the rice — it is not burned; it is the prize. Replace the lid and let the rice rest off the heat for 10 minutes before serving.

name: Kofta
description: Hand-formed lamb and onion cylinders threaded on flat skewers, heavy with allspice and raw parsley — grilled over charcoal until the outside is dark and crackling while the inside stays pink-tinged and impossibly juicy.
ingredients: 1 medium brown onion, grated on large holes
½ cup flat-leaf parsley, very finely chopped
½ teaspoon Aleppo pepper flakes or red chilli flakes
steps: Grate the onion on the large side of a box grater directly into a bowl, then squeeze out as much liquid as possible — wet onion will make the kofta fall off the skewer. Combine with lamb, parsley, baharat, cumin, salt, and Aleppo pepper. Mix with your hands for a full 3 minutes, working and folding the mixture as though kneading bread. The mixture should become sticky and cohesive, almost elastic, as the myosin proteins bind. Refrigerate for 30 minutes to firm.

With wet hands, take roughly 90g of mixture (about the size of a golf ball) and press firmly around a flat metal skewer, moulding it into a cylinder about 12 cm long and 3 cm wide. Press hard enough to eliminate any air pockets — squeeze from the centre outward. Press the ends firmly closed. The kofta should feel solid and dense, not hollow. If using bamboo skewers, soak in water 30 minutes first. Alternatively, shape into patties for pan-frying.

Grill over very high, direct charcoal or gas heat. Do not touch for the first 3–4 minutes — let the kofta sear and release naturally from the grill. Turn once, cook another 3–4 minutes. Total cook time is 7–9 minutes for medium (still pink inside), which is the traditional target. An internal temperature of 63 C is medium. Rest on a rack for 3 minutes before serving with warm pita, tahini, and fattoush.

name: Korean Fried Chicken
description: The double-fry is not a technique — it is a philosophy. First fry sets the crust and begins rendering the fat; second fry shatters the crust into something approaching glass, a shell so thin and crisp it crackles audibly across a room. The yangnyeom sauce — a lacquer of gochujang, honey, and garlic — clings without softening it, and the whole thing glows under kitchen light like lacquerware.
ingredients: 10 chicken wings or drumettes, or bone-in pieces (2 lb)
4 cups neutral oil for deep frying, canola or rice bran
3 tablespoons gochujang, Korean fermented red chile paste
4 garlic cloves, minced to a paste
1 tablespoon toasted sesame seeds and sliced scallions
steps: Pat chicken completely dry with paper towels — this is non-negotiable. Season with salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Toss to coat evenly. Let stand at room temperature for 30 minutes, or refrigerate uncovered for up to 2 hours for a drier surface and crispier result. The drier the surface, the crispier the crust.

Whisk potato starch and flour together in a wide bowl. Add cold water and mix until a thin, lumpy batter forms — do not overmix. The batter should be thinner than pancake batter and slightly lumpy. Add the seasoned chicken pieces and toss to coat thoroughly. Some pieces will have a thin, irregular coat; others will have drips and ridges — this inconsistency creates the craggly, ultra-crispy surface. Let battered chicken rest 5 minutes.

Heat oil to 330 F (165 C) in a deep pot. Fry the battered chicken in uncrowded batches for 8-10 minutes until lightly golden and cooked through. Remove and drain on a wire rack — not paper towels. Rest 10 minutes. Increase oil temperature to 375 F (190 C). Fry the same pieces a second time for 3-4 minutes until they turn deep amber-gold and audibly crackle when lifted from the oil. Remove and drain immediately.

Combine gochujang, honey, brown sugar, garlic paste, soy sauce, sesame oil, and rice vinegar in a small saucepan. Warm over medium heat, stirring, until the sugar dissolves and the sauce barely simmers — about 2 minutes. Do not boil. Working quickly, add the double-fried chicken to a large bowl and pour the warm sauce over. Toss rapidly to coat every piece. Garnish with sesame seeds and scallions. Serve within 5 minutes — the crust stays crisp for about 10 minutes after saucing.

name: Korean Haemul Pajeon
description: A wide, golden seafood and green onion pancake with a shatteringly crisp exterior and a tender, eggy interior — the kind of thing every Korean home makes when the first rain of the season falls.
ingredients: 2 bunches of green onions, trimmed to pan length; scallions (200 g)
1 cup raw shrimp, peeled and roughly chopped (150 g)
100 g squid, cleaned and cut into rings
¼ cup neutral oil, sunflower or corn (60 ml)
2 tablespoons soy sauce, for dipping sauce (30 ml)
2 teaspoons rice vinegar, for dipping sauce
1¼ teaspoons gochugaru, Korean chili flakes, for dipping
steps: Whisk together the all-purpose flour and rice flour in a large bowl. Beat the eggs into the ice-cold water separately, then pour into the flour. Stir with chopsticks or a fork until just combined — lumps are fine and even desirable; overmixing develops gluten which makes the pancake chewy rather than crisp. The batter should be the consistency of thin cream. The cold water is critical: cold batter = crisp pajeon.

Fold the green onions (arranged lengthwise if possible), shrimp, and squid into the batter. The batter should just coat everything — you should be able to see the green onions distinctly through the batter, not buried under a thick coating. Prepare the dipping sauce by combining soy sauce, rice vinegar, sugar, and gochugaru in a small bowl.

Heat a large (25–30cm) non-stick or cast-iron skillet over medium-high heat until very hot. Add 3 tbsp of the oil — it should shimmer immediately. Pour in all the batter at once and spread it quickly into a round using the back of a spoon. Reduce heat to medium. Press the pancake firmly with a spatula every minute to compress it and encourage even contact with the pan. Cook for 5–6 minutes until the underside is deeply golden-brown and crisp. Drizzle the remaining oil around the edges. Flip in one decisive motion and press firmly again. Cook 3–4 minutes on the second side. Serve immediately, cut into wedges, with the dipping sauce.

name: Sigeumchi Namul (Korean Sesame Spinach)
description: Blanched spinach squeezed to silk and dressed in toasted sesame, garlic, and soy — the simplest banchan in the Korean table, and the one that disappears first from the bowl.
ingredients: A bunch of fresh spinach, whole leaf, not baby (300 g)
1 tablespoon soy sauce, tamari for gluten-free
steps: Bring a large pot of generously salted boiling water to a rolling boil. Add the spinach all at once and blanch for 30–45 seconds — just until fully wilted and vivid green. Do not blanch longer. Immediately drain and transfer to a bowl of ice water to stop the cooking and set the color. After 1 minute, drain and squeeze the spinach firmly with both hands to remove as much water as possible. The squeezed bundle should be about a third of the original volume. Cut the bundle twice crosswise into thirds.

Place the cut spinach in a bowl. Add the soy sauce, toasted sesame oil, and minced raw garlic. Toss with your hands, working the dressing into every layer of the spinach. Taste and adjust — the spinach should be well-seasoned and savory, with the sesame oil perfuming every bite. The raw garlic will mellow slightly as the namul sits. For a milder version, very briefly sauté the garlic in the sesame oil before adding.

Transfer the seasoned spinach to a small serving bowl. Scatter the toasted sesame seeds over the top. Serve at room temperature or slightly chilled as a banchan alongside rice and other Korean dishes. Sigeumchi namul improves after 30 minutes as the flavors meld — it is an ideal make-ahead dish and keeps refrigerated for up to 3 days.

name: Kung Pao Chicken (Gong Bao Ji Ding)
description: Cubed chicken thigh, quick-velveted in cornstarch, meets a fiercely hot wok alongside dried Sichuan chilies and fried peanuts in a sauce that balances the four elements of Sichuan cuisine — numbing, hot, sour, and sweet — in a single chopstick load. The chilies go in whole and stay whole: their job is to perfume the oil, not disintegrate into the dish.
ingredients: 3 boneless chicken thighs, skin-off, cut into 2 cm cubes (400 g)
1 tablespoon light soy sauce, for marinade
2 teaspoons Shaoxing rice wine, for marinade
2 dried Sichuan red chilies, whole, stems on
½ cup roasted unsalted peanuts (60 g)
2 scallions, cut into 2 cm sections (30 g)
A knob of fresh ginger, minced
1½ tablespoons light soy sauce, for sauce (20 ml)
1½ teaspoons cornstarch mixed with cold water, 1:2, for sauce
steps: Cut the chicken thighs into 2 cm cubes, aiming for uniform size so they cook evenly in the wok. Combine with the cornstarch, soy sauce, and Shaoxing wine in a bowl. Toss thoroughly until every piece is coated in the thick, slightly sticky marinade. This is the 'velveting' technique — the cornstarch forms a protective coating that prevents the chicken from overcooking and drying out during high-heat stir-frying, and creates a very faint, smooth skin that catches the sauce. Let it rest for at least 20 minutes at room temperature. The soy and wine will begin to penetrate the surface of the chicken, and the cornstarch will fully hydrate. Do not refrigerate for this short marinade — cold chicken going into a hot wok drops the wok temperature dramatically and steams rather than sears. While the chicken marinates, mix the sauce in a small bowl: combine the soy sauce for sauce, black vinegar, and sugar and stir until the sugar dissolves. Set aside. The sauce should taste aggressively sour-sweet-salty, since it will be diluted by the wok's heat and the chicken's juices.

Heat the neutral oil in your wok over medium-high heat until it begins to shimmer and you can see faint wisps of heat rising from the surface — about 175°C. Add the whole dried Sichuan chilies and the Sichuan peppercorns together. They will immediately spit and crackle. Stir continuously and briskly with a wok spatula for 20–30 seconds. This is the blooming stage: the dry heat extracts the fat-soluble capsaicin from the chilies and the hydroxy-alpha-sanshool (the numbing compound) from the peppercorns into the oil, perfuming the entire cooking medium with mala (numbing-hot) flavor. The chilies should deepen from bright red to a dark, brick-wine red — not black. The peppercorns will turn a darker, more fragrant shade. Your kitchen will immediately fill with a sharp, throat-catching, floral chili vapor. This is normal and desirable: it means the oil is absorbing the flavor.

Working quickly — kung pao is a high-speed dish and every second matters. Into the chili oil, add the garlic, ginger, and scallion sections and stir-fry for 15 seconds until fragrant. Raise the heat to maximum. Add the velveted chicken in a single layer and let it sear undisturbed for 60 seconds — you need the high heat to develop a faint crust on the cornstarch coating. Then stir-fry vigorously, tossing constantly, for another 2–3 minutes until the chicken is just cooked through. Test by cutting a cube — the center should be white with no pink. Pour the pre-mixed sauce (soy, vinegar, sugar) around the edges of the wok where it will hit the hottest surfaces and caramelize slightly as it enters the dish. Stir everything together for 30 seconds. Pour the cornstarch slurry in a thin stream around the edges, tossing as you pour, until the sauce tightens and clings to the chicken. Remove from heat. Add the roasted peanuts and toss once. The peanuts go in last to preserve their crunch. Serve immediately over steamed white rice.

name: Leeks Vinaigrette
description: Whole braised leeks, their layers softened to silk, served at room temperature beneath a sharp Dijon vinaigrette that pools in their cross-section rings — a brasserie dish of austere elegance, best when the leeks are barely warm and the vinaigrette is cold.
ingredients: 6 medium leeks, white and light-green parts only
½ teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground
steps: Trim the root end and any tough dark-green tops from each leek. Split each lengthwise from the top to within 2 cm of the root end, leaving them attached at the base. Fan open and wash under cold running water to remove all grit between the layers. Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a boil. Tie the leeks loosely in pairs with kitchen twine to keep them together. Lower into the water. Cook at a gentle boil for 18 to 22 minutes until completely tender throughout.

Lay the cooked leeks on a folded kitchen towel or rack in a single layer. Remove the twine. Let them cool to room temperature — about 20 minutes. Do not refrigerate. Press them gently to extract some of the cooking water, but do not squeeze hard enough to damage the layers.

In a small bowl, combine the minced shallot, Dijon mustard, vinegar, salt, and pepper. Let stand for 5 minutes — the vinegar will soften the sharpness of the raw shallot. Then whisk constantly while drizzling in the olive oil in a thin, steady stream to form a stable emulsion. The vinaigrette should be thick and creamy, not broken or oily.

Arrange the cooled leeks cut-side up on a serving platter or individual plates. Spoon the vinaigrette generously over them, letting it pool in the cross-section rings. Scatter the chopped parsley over the top. If including the egg mimosa, press the hard-boiled egg through a sieve or crumble it finely by hand over the dressed leeks. Serve at room temperature.

name: Lemon-Herb Roasted Chicken Thighs
description: Bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs roasted at high heat until the skin shatters like lacquered glass and the fat underneath has rendered completely into the meat. The lemon zest and herb paste rubbed under the skin blooms and perfumes the fat as it renders, so every bite tastes of thyme and citrus from the inside out.
ingredients: 1 lemon zest + juice, from 1 lemon; half the lemon
4 garlic cloves, minced to a paste
½ teaspoon freshly cracked black pepper
2 wedges of lemon wedges, for serving
steps: Mix olive oil, lemon zest, thyme, rosemary, garlic paste, salt, and pepper into a paste. Pat the chicken thighs completely dry with paper towels — this is the most important step for crispy skin. Gently loosen the skin from each thigh and push a portion of the herb paste directly under the skin, spreading it over the meat. Rub the remaining paste over the top and underside of each thigh. Place on a wire rack set over a rimmed baking sheet. Let stand at room temperature for 30 minutes (or refrigerate uncovered overnight for even crispier skin).

Preheat the oven to 425 F (220 C). Place the wire rack with thighs on the middle rack — do not crowd. Roast for 35-40 minutes without opening the oven or flipping. The skin will slowly render and crisp as the thighs cook through. In the final 5 minutes, squeeze the lemon juice directly over the thighs and increase to broil for 2-3 minutes to finish the skin. Target internal temperature: 165 F at the thickest part, away from the bone.

Transfer the thighs from the rack directly to a serving plate — never back into a pan where steam could re-soften the skin. Rest for 5 minutes uncovered. This short rest allows the juices to redistribute from the bone outward and the skin to firm from the residual heat. Serve with lemon wedges on the side.

name: Lomo Saltado
description: Peru's definitive chifa stir-fry — strips of sirloin and tomato hit in a screaming-hot wok with soy sauce and vinegar, tossed with fried potatoes and red onion into a juicy, smoky, uniquely Peruvian fusion dish.
ingredients: 600 g beef sirloin or tenderloin, sliced 1cm thick against the grain
2 yellow potatoes, cut into thick fries; Yukon Gold or similar (400 g)
2 red onions, cut into thick wedges; 8 wedges per onion (250 g)
3 ripe tomatoes, cut into thick wedges (300 g)
2 tablespoons ají amarillo paste, or 1 fresh ají amarillo, seeded and sliced (30 g)
½ cup vegetable oil, for frying and wok (120 g)
A handful of fresh coriander, roughly chopped; cilantro (20 g)
¾ teaspoon fine sea salt and black pepper
1⅔ cups cooked white rice, to serve (300 g)
steps: Heat about 4cm of vegetable oil in a large deep pot or wok to 175C / 350F. Test with a potato strip — it should sizzle immediately and vigorously. Fry the potato strips in batches, never crowding the oil, for 6–8 minutes per batch until cooked through and golden on the outside. Transfer to a wire rack set over paper towel and season immediately with salt while hot — the salt adheres to the hot potato surface. Do not cover; you want them to stay crisp. These potatoes will be added back to the wok at the end. This double-presence of fries and rice in a single dish is one of the things that makes lomo saltado uniquely Peruvian — the carb abundance is intentional and joyful.

While the potatoes fry, season the beef strips with ground cumin, salt, and black pepper. Toss to coat evenly. Let the beef sit at room temperature for 10 minutes — this isn't a long marinade but a short seasoning rest that lets the salt draw a small amount of moisture to the surface, which helps the meat sear faster and more evenly. Crucial point: the beef must be dry on the surface before it hits the wok. Pat it with paper towels if any moisture has pooled. Wet beef steams rather than sears, and the sear is everything in lomo saltado — it's what creates the signature smoky, charred edges that no amount of sauce can substitute.

Heat your wok or largest cast-iron skillet over the absolute highest heat your stove can produce for two full minutes. Add a thin film of vegetable oil and let it begin to smoke — this is the signal that you're at the right temperature. Add the beef strips in a single layer and leave them untouched for 60 seconds to develop a deep, dark sear. Toss once and sear for another 30 seconds. Remove the beef to a plate — you want it cooked to medium, not beyond. In the same screaming-hot wok (add a splash more oil if needed), add the red onion wedges and garlic. Toss constantly for 90 seconds — you want the onion to char slightly at the edges while staying crunchy at the core. Add the tomato wedges and ají amarillo paste, toss for 30 seconds, then return the beef. Pour the soy sauce and red wine vinegar directly into the center of the wok — they will spit, steam, and partially vaporize, creating the characteristic 'chifa smoke' of lomo saltado. Toss everything together vigorously for 60 seconds.

Add the fried potato strips to the wok and toss once with the stir-fried beef and vegetables — just once or twice; you want the potatoes to pick up the dark, glossy sauce without going soggy from excessive stirring. Scatter the fresh coriander over the top and toss again. Taste a piece of beef and a potato: the beef should be savory, slightly charred, warm-spiced from the cumin, with the sour brightness of vinegar; the potato should be crisp outside and carry a coating of the dark sauce. Serve immediately, piling directly alongside white rice. The potatoes should still have their crunch — lomo saltado waits for no one.

name: Mapo Tofu
description: Silken tofu bobbing in a rust-red sea of doubanjiang, fermented black beans, and ground pork — fiery, tingling, deeply savoury, and almost dangerously moreish. The Sichuan peppercorn delivers its signature ma (numbing) alongside the la (heat) of the chilies.
ingredients: 1⅔ cups silken or medium-firm tofu (400 g)
⅔ cup ground pork, 20% fat (150 g)
2½ tablespoons doubanjiang, Pixian broad bean chili paste (40 g)
1½ tablespoons fermented black beans, roughly chopped; douchi
A knob of fresh ginger, finely minced
1¼ teaspoons Sichuan peppercorns, toasted and ground
2 teaspoons dried chili flakes, Sichuan or Korean
1¼ cups chicken stock, or unsalted vegetable stock (300 ml)
1 tablespoon cornstarch, mixed with equal water; slurry
3 tablespoons neutral oil, vegetable or grapeseed (45 ml)
1 scallion, green parts only, thinly sliced (20 g)
steps: Cut the tofu into 2cm cubes and place carefully in a bowl. Bring a pot of lightly salted water to a gentle boil. Slide the tofu cubes in and blanch for 2 minutes — do not stir aggressively, as silken tofu shatters easily. Drain with a spider or slotted spoon onto a plate lined with kitchen paper. This step firms the tofu surface slightly, seasons it from within, and removes any beany off-flavours — it is the difference between mapo tofu with clean, distinct cubes and a broken, murky mess.

Heat the oil in a wok or wide heavy pan over high heat until wisps of smoke appear. Add the ground pork and spread it into a thin layer. Let it sear undisturbed for 90 seconds until the bottom is golden and fat has rendered. Break it up and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3–4 more minutes until all pink is gone and the pork has rendered its fat and some pieces are golden and slightly crisp. Do not drain the fat — it carries the chili and fermented flavour into the sauce.

Add the doubanjiang to the wok and stir-fry with the pork for 2 minutes over high heat until the paste darkens from red to a deep rust-brown and the oil in the wok turns a vivid crimson — this is the hallmark of properly fried doubanjiang. Add the fermented black beans, garlic, and ginger; stir-fry for 1 more minute. Add the dried chili flakes. The wok should smell intensely of fermented chili, garlic, and caramelised pork — deeply savoury and slightly harsh in the raw stage, which will mellow once the stock goes in.

Pour the stock into the wok and scrape up any stuck bits from the bottom. Bring to a simmer, then gently slide in the blanched tofu cubes using a spatula. Add the soy sauce. Stir by gently rocking the wok and using a spatula to move the sauce — never stir through the tofu with a spoon or it will shatter. Simmer gently for 4–5 minutes so the tofu absorbs the sauce from the outside inward. The sauce will thin from the tofu's water — the cornstarch slurry in the next step will bring it back.

Give the cornstarch slurry a quick stir (it settles fast) and pour it around the edge of the wok in a slow, thin stream, gently rocking the wok as you add it. Cook for 30–60 seconds until the sauce thickens to a glossy, coating consistency that clings to the tofu. Remove from heat. Sprinkle the toasted, ground Sichuan peppercorn over the top — do not add it during cooking, or the numbing compounds will dissipate. Scatter the sliced scallion. Serve immediately over steamed rice. The ma (numbing) sensation builds over 30–60 seconds after eating.

name: Menemen
description: Turkish eggs in spiced tomato — ripe tomatoes and sivri peppers sautéed until jammy and concentrated, then eggs poured directly in and folded gently until barely set, finished with a knob of butter, Aleppo pepper, and flat-leaf parsley. Breakfast, lunch, or late night — eaten from the pan with white bread.
ingredients: 3 ripe tomatoes, cored and roughly chopped (400 g)
¾ green sivri peppers or Italian frying pepper, sliced (150 g)
Half a white onion, finely diced; optional — contested (80 g)
2½ teaspoons Aleppo pepper, or mild red pepper flakes, pul biber
¾ teaspoon black pepper, freshly cracked
A handful of flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped
steps: Heat the butter and olive oil together in a wide, shallow pan — ideally a sahan (copper pan) or small cast-iron skillet, 22–24cm — over medium heat. If using onion, add it first and cook for 3–4 minutes until translucent. Add the sliced sivri peppers and cook, stirring occasionally, for 5–7 minutes until the peppers are completely soft, limp, and faintly blistered at the edges. The peppers should be almost sweet by this point — green pepper's bitterness cooks away with time. Season with a pinch of salt.

Add the roughly chopped tomatoes to the peppers, along with half the Aleppo pepper, the salt, and the black pepper. Stir to combine. Increase the heat to medium-high and cook, stirring occasionally and breaking up the tomato pieces with a wooden spoon, for 8–12 minutes until the tomatoes have completely collapsed and the mixture is thick, jammy, and reduced — the water has evaporated and the mixture is clinging to the pan rather than flowing freely. The sauce should be deeply coloured and fragrant.

Beat the eggs lightly in a bowl — just enough to break the yolks and roughly combine, leaving streaks of white visible (these streaks create a marbled effect in the finished dish). Pour the eggs directly over the tomato and pepper base. Using a silicone spatula, fold the eggs gently through the tomato base in slow, wide strokes — pull from the edges inward, letting the tomato base streak through the eggs. Alternatively, leave the eggs mostly whole for a different style: nest the eggs whole on top and cover with a lid for 3 minutes until the whites set but the yolks remain runny.

Remove the pan from the heat. Scatter the remaining Aleppo pepper generously over the top — it should look like a dusting of dark rust-red across the yellow-orange surface. Scatter the chopped parsley. Serve immediately in the pan — menemen is traditionally brought to the table in its cooking vessel with a stack of white bread alongside for tearing and scooping. Do not let it sit: the carry-over heat from the pan will continue cooking the eggs, and the difference between perfect and overcooked is measured in minutes.

name: Mujaddara (Lentils and Rice with Crispy Onion)
description: Earthen brown lentils and rice cooked together until they absorb and then share everything — finished with a crown of deeply caramelized onions so crisp they shatter and so sweet they taste of burnt sugar.
ingredients: 1 cup brown or green lentils, rinsed (200 g)
¾ cup long-grain white rice, rinsed; basmati (150 g)
3 large yellow onions, halved and thinly sliced (500 g)
steps: Heat the olive oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pan over medium-high heat. Add all the sliced onions — the pan will be very full. Cook, stirring every 3–4 minutes, for 35–45 minutes. The onions will shrink dramatically, releasing water first, then slowly browning as the water evaporates. In the last 10 minutes, increase heat to high and stir more frequently as the onions caramelize. The goal is deeply browned, almost crispy onions that are sweet and complex. Remove two-thirds of the onions and set aside as the topping. Leave one-third in the pan.

In the same pan with the remaining one-third of the caramelized onions, add the ground cumin, coriander, and allspice. Stir for 30 seconds. Add the rinsed lentils and the water. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook for 15 minutes until the lentils are partially tender but still have a slight bite — they are not done yet. Season generously with salt.

Add the rinsed basmati rice to the partially cooked lentils and stir to combine. Check the water level — there should be enough to just cover the mixture by 1cm. Add a splash more if needed. Bring to a boil, then cover tightly and reduce heat to the lowest setting. Cook for 15 minutes. Do not lift the lid. Remove from heat and let steam, covered, for 10 more minutes. Fluff with a fork. The lentils and rice should be cooked through and have absorbed all the liquid.

Plate the mujaddara in a wide, shallow bowl or deep plate. Pile the reserved caramelized onions on top — do not stir them in; the contrast of the soft, spiced rice-and-lentil base with the crispy, sweet onion crown is the dish. Serve with plain yogurt, a salad of chopped tomato and cucumber, and warm flatbread.

name: Middle Eastern Rice Pilaf with Vermicelli
description: Thin vermicelli threads toasted in butter until amber, then cooked with long-grain rice into a fragrant pilaf scattered with golden pine nuts — the backbone of the Levantine table.
ingredients: 1½ cups long-grain white rice, basmati (300 g)
2¼ cups chicken or vegetable broth (550 ml)
A small handful of fresh flat-leaf parsley, chopped
steps: Rinse the rice in several changes of cold water until the water runs clear, releasing excess surface starch that would make the pilaf gluey. Cover with cold water and soak for 20 minutes. Drain thoroughly in a fine-mesh strainer and pat lightly dry — residual moisture will cause the butter to spatter.

Melt the butter in a heavy-bottomed saucepan over medium heat. Add the pine nuts and toss for 1–2 minutes until golden. Remove with a slotted spoon and set aside — they burn quickly. Add the broken vermicelli to the remaining butter and toss constantly for 3–4 minutes until the noodles turn a deep amber-brown and smell of toasted hazelnuts. This is the defining character of the dish.

Add the drained rice to the toasted vermicelli and stir to coat in the butter for 1 minute. Pour in the hot broth, add salt and allspice. Stir once. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to the lowest simmer, cover tightly, and cook for 15 minutes. Remove from heat and steam, covered, for 10 minutes. Do not lift the lid during cooking or steaming.

Fluff the pilaf with a fork, turning gently from the bottom up. Mound onto a warmed serving platter. Scatter the reserved golden pine nuts over the top and finish with the chopped parsley. Serve immediately.

name: Nasu Dengaku
description: Halved Japanese eggplant lacquered in a sweet-savory white miso glaze, broiled until the surface caramelizes to deep amber and the flesh beneath collapses to yielding silk. A dish of opposites — bitter char over honeyed umami, firm skin over trembling interior.
ingredients: ¼ cup white miso, shiro miso (60 g)
1 scallion, thinly sliced on the bias (20 g)
steps: Halve the eggplants lengthwise. Using a sharp paring knife, score the cut face in a deep crosshatch pattern — cut about two-thirds into the flesh at 1 cm intervals in both directions without piercing the skin. This scoring is critical: it allows heat to penetrate and sesame oil to seep into the flesh, preventing steam from splitting the skin and dramatically shortening the roasting time. Press the cut face lightly to open the grid slightly.

Brush the scored cut face generously with sesame oil, working the oil into the crosshatch cuts with the brush. Flip and brush a thin layer over the skin side as well. The sesame oil serves double duty: it prevents sticking and imparts a deep, nutty fragrance that suffuses the flesh during roasting. Line a baking tray with foil and place eggplant halves cut-side down.

Roast cut-side down in a 220°C (425°F) oven for 12–15 minutes, until the flesh is completely tender when pierced with a chopstick or skewer and the cut faces have taken on a light gold color from contact with the tray. This initial roasting collapses the air pockets in the spongy eggplant flesh and drives out moisture, which concentrates the flavor and creates the right base for the glaze to adhere to. Do not rush this step — underdone eggplant will have a bitter, spongy bite.

While the eggplant roasts, combine white miso, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small saucepan over very low heat. Whisk constantly as the mixture warms — the goal is just to dissolve the sugar and bring everything into a smooth, homogeneous paste, not to cook it. The glaze should be warm, fluid, and spreadable, the consistency of thick yogurt. Remove from heat as soon as it is smooth. Taste: it should be deeply savory, sweetly balanced, and intensely fragrant.

Flip the roasted eggplant halves so the cut face is now up. Spoon the dengaku glaze generously over each half, spreading it to the edges with the back of the spoon. The layer should be thick enough to be opaque — roughly 3–4mm — so it caramelizes and chars slightly rather than burning off thin. Do not be timid: a thick, generous glaze is what makes this dish.

Broil the glazed eggplant halves under a hot broiler (or salamander) for 3–5 minutes, watching constantly. The glaze should bubble, then caramelize to deep amber-brown with slightly charred edges and spots — this Maillard browning and mild caramelization is the defining character of dengaku. Remove from the broiler and let rest for 1 minute on the tray. Transfer to serving plates, scatter toasted sesame seeds generously, and finish with sliced scallion. Serve immediately while the eggplant is still trembling-soft and the glaze is warm.

name: Miso-Roasted Sweet Potato
description: Japanese whole sweet potatoes roasted low and slow until their sugars caramelise from within, then split and glazed with a white miso and butter mixture that melts into every crack — the simplest of things, made luminous.
ingredients: 3 Japanese sweet potatoes or orange-flesh sweet potatoes, Satsumaimo (800 g)
¾ thinly sliced spring onion, green part only
steps: Preheat the oven to 180 C (355 F). Place the whole, unpeeled sweet potatoes directly on the oven rack with a foil-lined tray below to catch drips. Roast for 55–75 minutes depending on size (a chopstick pressed into the thickest part should meet no resistance). The skin will blister and deflate; a dark, caramelised syrup will drip from the ends.

While the potatoes roast, combine the softened butter, white miso, and mirin in a small bowl. Stir vigorously until completely smooth and homogenous. The mixture will be a pale amber paste. Set aside at room temperature.

Split each sweet potato lengthwise with a sharp knife — but not quite all the way through. Press the two ends toward each other to open up the split and create a cavity. Spoon or pipe a generous amount of the miso butter into the cavity. Finish under the grill (broiler) at high heat for 3–4 minutes until the glaze is bubbling and caramelised. Scatter flaky salt, sesame seeds, and spring onion.

name: Moqueca Baiana
description: A Bahian fish stew of intoxicating depth — white fish simmered in coconut milk and dendê palm oil with tomatoes, peppers, and cilantro, everything cooked in a heavy clay pot that holds the heat like a loving embrace.
ingredients: 4 firm white fish, 4 cm chunks fillets, e.g. sea bass or cod (600 g)
2 tablespoons lime juice, freshly squeezed (30 ml)
2½ tablespoons dendê oil, red palm (40 ml)
1 red and green bell pepper, thinly sliced (200 g)
A tin of full-fat coconut milk (400 ml)
A handful of fresh cilantro, stems and leaves separated (20 g)
steps: Toss fish chunks with lime juice, a pinch of salt, and minced garlic (half the garlic). Cover and refrigerate for 20-30 minutes. The acid will begin to set the exterior proteins, helping the fish hold together in the stew without falling apart.

Heat dendê oil in a heavy clay pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add onion and cook 5 minutes until soft and turning golden. Add remaining garlic and bell peppers and cook 3 more minutes. The dendê oil will turn the whole base a vivid orange — this is correct and beautiful.

Add tomatoes and cilantro stems to the sofrito. Cook 5 minutes until tomatoes begin to dissolve. Pour in coconut milk and stir. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat. Season well with salt and taste — the broth should be rich, sweet from coconut, and slightly acidic from the tomato.

Nestle the marinated fish gently into the simmering broth in a single layer. Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 8-12 minutes, depending on thickness. Do not stir — use the lid to baste. The fish is done when it flakes easily at the thickest point and is opaque throughout. Scatter cilantro leaves over the top and serve straight from the clay pot.
