name: Green Shakshuka
description: A tangle of wilted spinach, chard, and charred tomatillo collapses into a bright, acidic, deeply savory green sauce — then eggs are nestled into pockets and covered to set, their whites just barely opaque while the yolks remain trembling and liquid, waiting to break into the green.
ingredients: A bunch of baby spinach (200 g)
A bunch of swiss chard, stems and leaves separated (200 g)
½ cup feta cheese, crumbled (80 g)
¼ cup fresh cilantro, roughly chopped
¼ cup water or light vegetable stock (60 ml)
steps: Halve the tomatillos and place them cut-side down in a dry, ungreased heavy skillet (cast iron is ideal) over high heat. Do not stir. Let them char for 4-5 minutes until the cut surfaces are deeply blistered and black in spots, and the skins have softened and wrinkled. The sugars at the cut surface caramelize and char, converting tomatillo's raw, astringent sourness into something deeper, slightly sweet, and smoky. When a tomatillo releases from the pan easily when nudged with a spatula, it has charred correctly. Transfer them to a bowl — they will continue to soften from residual heat. The juices that leak into the bowl are precious: add them to the sauce.

In the same pan (leave any tomatillo char — it adds flavor), heat the olive oil over medium heat. Add the diced onion and the chard stems (chopped into 1 cm pieces) and cook, stirring occasionally, for 6-8 minutes until the onion is soft, translucent, and starting to turn golden at the edges. Add the sliced garlic and jalapeño and cook for 2 more minutes until fragrant. The garlic should turn golden at the edges but not brown — once it smells like roasted garlic rather than raw, you're there. Add the cumin and coriander and stir them directly into the oil for 30 seconds — this dry-blooms the spices in the fat and intensifies their fragrance by an order of magnitude. The pan should smell like a Moroccan kitchen.

Add the charred tomatillos (and all their juice) to the pan, pressing them with the back of a spoon to break them into rough pieces. Add the chard leaves (torn large) and the baby spinach — the pan will look impossibly full. Add the water and a generous pinch of salt. Cover and cook over medium heat for 4-5 minutes until the greens have completely wilted and collapsed. Remove the lid and stir everything together, breaking the tomatillos further into the sauce. Cook uncovered for 3-4 more minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce has thickened slightly and the greens have fully integrated. Taste and season generously — greens can absorb a surprising amount of salt. The sauce should be vivid green, slightly chunky, pleasantly sour from the tomatillo, and deeply savory.

Using the back of a large spoon, make six shallow wells in the green sauce, pressing down to the bottom of the pan. Crack an egg into a small cup first — this gives you control and prevents shell fragments. Slide each egg from the cup into its well. Scatter the crumbled feta around the eggs and into the sauce. Reduce heat to low, cover the pan with a lid or foil, and cook for 5-8 minutes, checking frequently. The whites should be just set — opaque and firm when you press the edge with a spoon — while the yolks remain visibly liquid and trembling. Remove from heat while the yolks still look underdone: residual heat continues cooking them for 1-2 minutes after the pan comes off the stove. Scatter the fresh cilantro over the top and serve directly from the pan with bread.

Scatter the fresh cilantro generously over the finished pan — the heat of the shakshuka will wilt it slightly on contact, releasing its fragrance. Serve the shakshuka directly from the pan at the table, with warm pita or crusty bread for tearing and dragging through the sauce. The protocol for eating: tear bread, drag through sauce capturing both green and white egg, ensure the final bite has yolk. The shakshuka is at peak quality for approximately 5 minutes after coming off the heat — the egg continues to cook from residual heat and firm progressively. Serve without ceremony.

name: Sinigang na Hipon
description: Philippines' definitive sour broth — head-on shrimp simmered with kangkong, tomatoes, daikon, and eggplant in a tamarind-bright soup that is at once light, tart, and deeply satisfying.
ingredients: 20 large raw shrimp, head-on and shell-ons (500 g)
¼ cup tamarind paste, or 1 packet sinigang mix (60 g)
¼ daikon radish, sliced 1 cm rounds (200 g)
1 Japanese eggplant, sliced into chunks (200 g)
⅔ cup water spinach or baby spinach, kangkong (150 g)
steps: Bring the water to a rolling boil in a large pot. Add the quartered onion and tomatoes. Boil vigorously for 8–10 minutes, pressing the tomatoes against the side of the pot occasionally with the back of a spoon to help them break down and release their juices into the water. The tomatoes are not just aromatic — they provide body and sweetness that frames the sour tamarind. The broth will turn a faint pinkish-orange as they dissolve.

Add the tamarind paste (or sinigang mix) and stir until fully dissolved. Taste the broth — it should be bracingly, pleasantly sour. Add the daikon rounds and eggplant chunks. Adjust the heat to a gentle simmer and cook for 10–12 minutes until the daikon is just tender when pierced with a chopstick. The eggplant will absorb the sour broth and become silky. Sinigang's sourness should make you pucker slightly but not wince.

Add the head-on shrimp and the whole green chiles to the simmering broth. The shrimp go in raw and cook quickly — 3–5 minutes depending on size. The heads will leach their coral-orange fat directly into the broth, enriching it with umami. Do not overcook: shrimp tighten quickly and become rubbery beyond 5 minutes. Watch them change color and remove from heat the moment the last one turns fully pink.

Add the water spinach (or spinach) leaves and stems to the pot. They will wilt in 1–2 minutes — stalks first, leaves last. Season the broth with fish sauce and salt, adding them gradually and tasting after each addition. The final flavor profile should be bright and sour as the dominant note, with a salty umami backbone from the fish sauce and shrimp heads, and a background sweetness from the tomatoes. Serve immediately in deep bowls with steamed white rice on the side.

name: Spanakopita (Greek Spinach Pie)
description: Crisp, golden phyllo pastry layered with a filling of wilted spinach, crumbled feta, dill and egg — each shattering, paper-thin sheet giving way to the creamy, herby, salty filling within. The kind of pie that disappears the moment it reaches the table.
ingredients: 400 g phyllo dough, fresh or fully thawed
4 bunches of fresh spinach, or frozen 500g, fully thawed and squeezed (1000 g)
4 spring onions stalks, thinly sliced; scallions
2 handfuls of fresh dill, roughly chopped (30 g)
½ cup olive oil or melted unsalted butter, for brushing (120 ml)
¾ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
A pinch of freshly grated nutmeg
steps: If using fresh spinach, wilt it in a dry pan or with a splash of water over high heat until completely collapsed, then tip into a colander and cool. When cool enough to handle, squeeze the spinach in your fists — hard, relentlessly, handful by handful — until almost no water comes out. This is the most critical step in the recipe: residual spinach water makes the filling wet, turns the phyllo soggy, and ruins the finished pie. A kilogram of raw spinach will reduce to about 200g of dry, dark-green paste. Transfer to a large bowl and coarsely chop. Add the crumbled feta, beaten eggs, spring onions, dill, black pepper and nutmeg. Mix together with a fork until cohesive — the filling should look like a rough, green-flecked, salty mixture, not a smooth paste. Taste (carefully — the feta is already salty) and add more pepper or dill as needed. Set aside.

Preheat the oven to 190°C / 375°F. Brush a 30×22cm (or equivalent) baking pan generously with oil or melted butter. Work with phyllo quickly — it dries and tears within minutes of exposure to air; keep the stack covered with a damp towel between sheets. Lay the first sheet of phyllo in the pan, letting the excess hang over the edges. Brush the entire surface generously with oil or butter, reaching all the way to the edges and corners. Lay another sheet perpendicular to the first, brush again. Repeat this layering and brushing process until you have used roughly half the phyllo sheets (8–10 sheets depending on thickness). The fat between each layer is what creates the shatter-crisp, separated layers of the finished crust — do not skimp.

Spread the filling evenly across the phyllo base using a spatula, pressing it into an even layer and tucking it into the corners. Fold the overhanging phyllo edges inward over the filling — they will form part of the top crust. Now layer the remaining phyllo sheets over the top in the same oiled fashion, sheet by sheet, each one brushed generously. Fold or tuck the overhanging top sheets under the pie to form a neat border. Brush the entire top surface very generously with oil. Score the top layers only with a sharp knife in the portion sizes you want before baking — the classic diamond or square patterns — cutting through only the top 4–5 sheets, not all the way through to the filling. This prevents the crust from shattering uncontrollably when you cut after baking.

Bake at 190°C / 375°F for 45–55 minutes until the top is a deep, even golden-brown across its entire surface. Rotate the pan once at the halfway mark to ensure even browning. The pie is done when the scored lines have opened up and the phyllo between them has puffed and crisped, the edges are a slightly darker amber, and the kitchen smells of buttered pastry and herbs. Rest for at least 10 minutes before cutting along the pre-scored lines — the filling needs a moment to firm from liquid-eggy to sliceable. Serve warm or at room temperature; it is equally magnificent both ways.

name: Spanish Clams with Chorizo and White Wine
description: Littleneck clams steam open in a broth of smoky chorizo fat, white wine, and garlic — the most effortless dish in the Spanish canon, and the one most likely to make you forget everything else you planned to cook.
ingredients: 1 cup Spanish chorizo, cured, sliced into coins (150 g)
¾ cup dry white wine, Albariño or Verdejo (200 ml)
A handful of flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped
1¼ teaspoons smoked paprika, pimentón de la Vera
steps: Soak the clams in cold, lightly salted water (30g salt per liter) for 30 minutes. The clams will expel any sand and grit they are holding. Drain and scrub the shells under cold running water. Discard any clam with a cracked shell or any that does not close when tapped — these are dead and will ruin the dish. Sort through them one by one; a single bad clam can make the entire broth bitter and unpleasant.

Heat the olive oil in a wide, heavy pan with a lid over medium heat. Add the chorizo coins and cook for 2–3 minutes until the fat renders and the oil turns a vivid orange-red from the paprika in the chorizo. Add the sliced garlic and smoked paprika, cooking for 60 seconds until fragrant. Do not let the garlic brown. This rendered chorizo fat is the foundation of the entire dish.

Add the scrubbed clams to the pan and immediately pour in the white wine. Cover tightly and raise the heat to high. Cook for 4–5 minutes, shaking the pan once or twice. Begin checking at 4 minutes — the moment all (or nearly all) the clams are open, they are done. Remove the lid and add the parsley and lemon juice. Toss quickly and serve in deep bowls with crusty bread to mop the broth. Discard any clam that has not opened after 6 minutes — it was dead before cooking.

name: Mediterranean Stuffed Bell Peppers
description: Sweet red peppers stuffed with herbed rice, pine nuts, and currants, baked until the peppers soften and collapse around their fragrant filling.
ingredients: 1 cup long-grain white rice, rinsed (200 g)
A handful of fresh mint, chopped
A handful of flat-leaf parsley, chopped
¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil (60 ml)
steps: Bring a saucepan of salted water to a boil. Add the rinsed rice and cook for exactly 7 minutes — you want the rice half-cooked, still chalky in the center. Drain well and spread on a tray to stop cooking.

Warm the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and translucent, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and pine nuts; cook 2–3 minutes until the pine nuts are lightly golden. Stir in the currants, cinnamon, and salt. Remove from heat.

Combine the sautéed base with the parboiled rice, mint, and parsley. Toss to distribute evenly. Taste — the filling should be assertively seasoned, as the rice will absorb salt from the passata during baking. Cut the tops off the peppers and remove seeds and membranes. Fill each pepper about three-quarters full — the rice will expand.

Pour the tomato passata into the base of the baking dish around the peppers. Drizzle olive oil over the tops. Cover tightly with foil and bake at 180°C (350°F) for 40 minutes. Remove foil and bake a further 15 minutes until the pepper skins are wrinkled, tender, and slightly charred at the tips.

name: Southern Succotash
description: A summer jubilee of sweet corn, lima beans, and cherry tomatoes cooked in bacon fat — humble vegetables made rich and textured, finished with butter and herbs.
ingredients: 2¾ cups fresh sweet corn kernels, from about 4 ears (400 g)
2 cups baby lima beans, fresh or frozen (300 g)
⅔ cup streaky bacon, sliced into lardons (100 g)
¾ white onion, finely diced (120 g)
A small handful of fresh basil, torn
¾ teaspoon freshly cracked black pepper
steps: Place bacon lardons in a cold, wide skillet or cast-iron pan. Set over medium heat and cook, stirring occasionally, until the fat has rendered completely and the bacon is deeply browned and crisp — about 8–10 minutes. Scoop the bacon out with a slotted spoon onto paper towels. Leave the rendered fat in the pan.

In the same pan with the rendered bacon fat, add the onion and cook over medium heat until softened and just beginning to turn golden, about 5 minutes. Add the corn kernels and lima beans along with the thyme. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the corn is tender and starting to blister in patches and the lima beans are heated through and creamy — about 6–8 minutes.

Add the garlic and halved cherry tomatoes to the pan. Cook just 2 minutes — enough for the tomato skins to just begin to blister and split without losing their shape. Remove from heat. Add the cold butter and swirl the pan to melt and emulsify it into the vegetables. Season generously with salt and pepper. Scatter the torn basil and crumble the reserved crisp bacon over the top. Serve immediately.

name: Swordfish alla Ghiotta
description: Swordfish steaks braised Sicilian-style in a sweet-sour agrodolce sauce of olives, capers, cherry tomatoes, celery, pine nuts and raisins — the flavors of a Palermo mercato distilled into a single fragrant pan. Bittersweet, briny, and unmistakably marine.
ingredients: ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil (60 ml)
½ cup green Castelvetrano olives, pitted and halved (80 g)
3½ tablespoons capers, salted or in brine; rinsed; drained (30 g)
A small handful of fresh mint leaves
steps: Pat the swordfish steaks very dry and season both sides generously with salt and pepper. Heat half the olive oil in a wide, heavy skillet over high heat until just smoking. Sear the swordfish for 2–3 minutes per side until a golden-brown crust forms on both faces. The fish will not be cooked through — you are building the crust and the fond, not finishing the fish. Remove to a plate. The fish will finish in the sauce.

In the same skillet, reduce to medium heat and add the remaining oil. Add the onion and celery. Cook, stirring, for 6–8 minutes until completely soft and the onion is translucent and just beginning to turn golden. Add the pine nuts and cook 2 minutes until lightly toasted — they will pick up golden color and smell of toasted wood and fat. Add the raisins and stir for 30 seconds until they plump slightly.

Add the cherry tomatoes, olives, and rinsed capers to the pan. Stir and cook for 3 minutes until the tomatoes begin to break down and release their juice. In a small bowl, dissolve the sugar in the wine vinegar, then pour over the pan. Stir to combine. The sauce will immediately smell sharp and bright from the vinegar. Simmer for 4–5 minutes until the sauce has thickened slightly and the sharp edge of the raw vinegar has mellowed into something sweet-sour and rounded.

Nestle the seared swordfish steaks into the sauce, spooning some sauce over the top of each one. Cover the pan and braise over low heat for 6–8 minutes, depending on thickness. The sauce will steam the fish gently from above while the residual heat from below finishes the interior. Uncover and check: the fish should be just barely opaque throughout, still slightly yielding at the very center. Do not overcook — swordfish dries out fast. Tear fresh mint leaves over the top and serve from the pan.

name: Tabouli
description: Lebanon's great herb salad — an enormous, verdant mass of flat-leaf parsley and mint, finely hand-chopped, with only a small quantity of fine bulgur soaked (never cooked), dressed aggressively with lemon juice and olive oil; the grain is an accent, the parsley is everything.
ingredients: 5 bunches of flat-leaf parsley, 4 large bunches, leaves and fine stems only (200 g)
2 handfuls of fresh mint leaves (30 g)
¼ cup fine bulgur wheat, #1 grade (50 g)
1¼ cups ripe tomatoes, finely diced, drained of excess juice (300 g)
4 scallions, white and pale green parts, thinly sliced (60 g)
⅓ cup fresh lemon juice, about 3 lemons (80 ml)
¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil (60 ml)
¾ teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground
steps: Place the fine bulgur in a small bowl. Pour half the lemon juice (40 ml) directly over it — soaking in lemon juice rather than water means the bulgur absorbs acidity as it hydrates, so it is never bland or watery. Add just enough cold water to barely cover the grain (about 50 ml). Stir once and leave to soak for 20 minutes. After soaking, tip the bulgur into the center of a clean kitchen towel or several layers of cheesecloth and wring firmly — extracting as much liquid as possible. The bulgur must be as dry as you can make it, or it will water down the salad.

Wash and thoroughly dry the parsley and mint — wet herbs will release water into the salad. Use a sharp chef's knife only — never a food processor, which bruises the leaves and turns them dark and bitter within minutes. Gather the parsley into a tight bundle and chop fine with a rocking motion, then rotate 90 degrees and chop again. The goal is a fine, green confetti — not a paste, not rough chunks. Chop the mint separately (it is more delicate) and fold it in. The volume of herb should be approximately 4-5 times the volume of everything else; if you feel you have too much parsley, you are probably correct.

Dice the tomatoes into small cubes, no larger than 5 mm. Place the diced tomatoes in a fine-mesh sieve or colander and let them drain for 10 minutes — tomatoes release a lot of water, and undrained tomatoes will pool at the bottom of the salad within minutes of serving. Slice the scallions into thin rounds. The scallion provides the onion note in tabouli — raw white onion is traditional in some versions, but scallions are milder and more commonly used in modern Lebanese kitchens.

In a large mixing bowl, combine the chopped herbs, squeezed-dry bulgur, drained tomatoes, and scallions. Drizzle the remaining lemon juice and olive oil over everything. Add the allspice, cinnamon, salt, and pepper. Toss gently but thoroughly using two large spoons or clean hands, lifting from the bottom and turning — you are not trying to crush anything, just coat every element in the dressing. The salad will compress slightly as it is tossed. Taste: tabouli should be aggressively, almost bracingly lemony. If it seems too mild, add more lemon juice.

Taste the dressed tabouli and adjust. The correct seasoning for tabouli is different from most dishes: the lemon must be the loudest note — if you are hesitant, add more. The olive oil should be present but should not make the salad heavy. The allspice and cinnamon are subtle warmth, not detectable as distinct spices. Salt should make everything pop without being perceptible on its own. Let the tabouli rest at room temperature for 15 minutes before serving — this brief rest allows the salt to draw a small amount of moisture from the herbs, which mingles with the dressing and creates the finished sauce.

name: Baja Fish Tacos
description: Beer-battered white fish from the Baja California coast — impossibly light, shatteringly crisp, tucked into warm corn tortillas with shredded cabbage, chipotle crema, and a squeeze of lime that cuts through the richness like a knife. Street food at its most honest.
ingredients: 4 firm white fish, skinless fillets, mahi-mahi, cod, or halibut (600 g)
¾ cup ice-cold lager beer (200 ml)
1 L neutral oil for deep-frying, vegetable or sunflower
2⅓ cups green cabbage, finely shredded (200 g)
½ cup Mexican crema or sour cream (120 ml)
1 tablespoon chipotle peppers in adobo, minced (20 g)
A handful of fresh cilantro, roughly torn (20 g)
Pickled jalapeños or fresh salsa, to taste
steps: Whisk minced chipotles in adobo into the crema until fully combined. Start with half the chipotle and taste — it should be smoky, creamy, and moderately spicy. The heat blooms after a minute of contact, so taste again before adding more. Transfer to a squeeze bottle or small bowl. Refrigerate until ready to use.

Whisk flour, baking powder, salt, cumin, and paprika together in a wide bowl. Make a well in the center and pour in the ice-cold beer all at once. Whisk just until combined — lumps are welcome, overworking builds gluten and the batter will be tough. The batter should be the consistency of thin pancake batter. Keep the batter cold; set the bowl over ice if your kitchen is warm.

Heat oil in a deep, heavy pot to 185°C (365°F). Cut fish into strips about 2.5 cm × 8 cm. Pat completely dry. Working in batches of 4–5 strips, dip each piece in batter, let excess drip for 2 seconds, then lower gently into the oil. Fry for 3–4 minutes, turning once, until the batter is deep golden and the fish floats freely. Drain on a wire rack over a sheet pan — never on paper towel, which steams the crust soft.

Warm tortillas directly on a gas flame or dry hot griddle until pliable and slightly charred at the edges. Double them up (traditional Baja style prevents sogginess). Layer: a pinch of raw cabbage, 2–3 strips of hot fish, a drizzle of chipotle crema, a scattering of cilantro, and a stripe of salsa or pickled jalapeños. Finish with a hard squeeze of lime. Eat immediately — the crust on the fish is a living, dying thing that begins to soften the moment it is dressed.

name: Kerala Tamarind Prawn Curry
description: Kerala-style prawn curry where shrimp simmer in a tangy, deeply spiced tamarind-coconut gravy with curry leaves, mustard seeds, turmeric, and dried red chiles — the sour tamarind balanced by sweet coconut and pungent fenugreek.
ingredients: 3⅓ cups raw prawns, peeled and deveined (500 g)
¾ cup full-fat coconut milk (200 ml)
A knob of fresh ginger, minced (20 g)
4 dried red chiles, Kashmiri or byadagi
1 teaspoon red chile powder, or cayenne
steps: Heat the coconut oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the mustard seeds — they will pop and splutter within seconds, scattering against the lid, so have it ready. As soon as the popping slows, add the fenugreek seeds, dried red chiles, and curry leaves in that order. The curry leaves will erupt violently in the hot oil, releasing their aromatic oils in a crackling burst. Stir once and allow 20–30 seconds for the fenugreek to toast to a pale gold.

Add the finely sliced onions to the spiced oil and stir to coat. Cook over medium heat, stirring regularly, for 10–12 minutes until the onions have melted down from their raw volume by more than half and turned a deep, even golden-brown — not blond, not mahogany. Add the garlic and ginger and fry for 2 minutes more, stirring constantly, until the raw smell of garlic cooks out and the mixture becomes sticky and fragrant.

Add the ground turmeric, coriander, and red chile powder to the golden onion base and stir vigorously to combine. Cook the spice mixture in the oil and onion paste for 90 seconds to 2 minutes, stirring constantly. This step — called bhunao in Hindi — fries the ground spices in fat, toasting them and driving off their raw notes. The mixture will look dry and clumpy at first, then loosen slightly as the spice oils release. Add a tablespoon of water if the spices begin to scorch.

Add the tamarind paste and stir it into the masala — it will hiss and sizzle. Pour in the coconut milk and salt, then stir thoroughly to combine everything into a smooth, uniform gravy. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered for 5–6 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the gravy has thickened slightly and the raw sour edge of the tamarind has mellowed into the coconut. Taste: the gravy should be sour, warm with spice, lightly sweet from the coconut, and well-salted.

Add the peeled prawns to the simmering gravy in a single layer, pressing them down to submerge. Scatter a few fresh curry leaves over the top. Cook for 4–5 minutes over medium heat, turning the prawns once at the halfway mark, until they are fully pink and just cooked through. Remove from heat immediately — the residual heat of the gravy will continue cooking them if left on the stove. Serve with Kerala red rice, appam, or roti.

name: Vegetable Tempura
description: Disparate vegetables coated in an ice-cold, barely-mixed batter and plunged into oil at exactly the right temperature — emerging in a gossamer-thin, shatteringly crisp shell so delicate it is nearly transparent, the vegetable's own steam driving pockets of airy lightness beneath.
ingredients: 600 g mixed vegetables: sweet potato, shiitake, green beans, lotus root, red pepper; sliced
¾ cup cake flour or all-purpose flour, very cold (120 g)
¼ cup potato starch or cornstarch (30 g)
¾ cup ice-cold sparkling or still water (180 ml)
1500 ml neutral oil for frying, sesame-sunflower blend or canola
¾ teaspoon fine salt, for dusting vegetables
steps: Prepare vegetables: slice sweet potato 6mm thick, clean shiitake and score the caps, top and tail green beans, slice lotus root 5mm thick, cut red pepper into wide strips. Pat all vegetables completely dry — any surface moisture prevents batter adhesion and causes dangerous oil splatter. Dust lightly with flour (the second function flour serves after structural gluten — it acts as a primer for batter adhesion). Keep everything cold until the moment of frying.

This step must be done RIGHT BEFORE frying — never in advance. Combine the egg yolk with the ice-cold sparkling water and stir briefly. Add both flours at once and stir with chopsticks or a fork only 8–10 strokes. The batter must remain lumpy, floury, and obviously under-mixed. Large dry flour streaks are normal and desirable. Do not be tempted to mix until smooth — gluten development is the enemy of tempura.

Heat the oil to exactly 170–175 C (340–345 F) — use a thermometer. Dip each vegetable piece briefly in the batter (let excess drip for just 1 second) and lower into the oil. Fry in small batches to maintain oil temperature — too many pieces cools the oil and produces soggy results. Fry 2–3 minutes until the batter sets to a very pale, almost white-gold. Drain on a rack. Serve within 2 minutes.

name: Thai Basil Fried Rice (Khao Pad Krapao)
description: Day-old jasmine rice blasted in a searing wok with ground pork, fish sauce, oyster sauce, and enough Thai chilies to make the kitchen uncomfortable — then buried in an avalanche of holy basil that wilts to a glossy, anise-fragrant blanket. Topped with a fried egg whose lacey crisp edges are as important as the rice itself.
ingredients: 1⅔ cups day-old cooked jasmine rice, cold, separated (300 g)
⅔ cup ground pork, or coarsely hand-chopped pork shoulder (150 g)
1 bird's eye chili, sliced or smashed; prik kee noo; 3–6 to taste
1 tablespoon fish sauce, Tiparos or Megachef (20 g)
3 tablespoons neutral oil, vegetable or lard (40 g)
2 handfuls of Holy basil, leaves picked — Italian basil is a poor substitute; bai krapao (30 g)
½ teaspoon eggs, for frying; 1 per serving
steps: Heat a wok or large heavy skillet over the highest flame until smoke wisps from the surface — 2 minutes minimum. Add 30 g of the oil and swirl immediately. Add the garlic and chilies all at once and stir-fry for 20 seconds until the garlic is gold and the kitchen fills with a sharp, peppery fragrance. Add the ground pork, breaking it up with a spatula. Let it sear undisturbed for 30 seconds, then break and toss. Cook for 2–3 minutes total until no pink remains and the pork has some golden, crumbly edges rather than being pale and steamed.

Add the cold rice to the wok, breaking up any clumps with the spatula before it hits the heat. Pour the fish sauce, oyster sauce, and soy sauce around the edge of the wok (not directly on the rice) so the sauces hit the hot metal and sizzle. Toss everything together vigorously for 2–3 minutes, pressing the rice flat against the wok surface for 20 seconds at a time to allow contact browning, then tossing to redistribute. The goal is every grain coated and slightly toasted, not steamed.

Remove the wok from heat. Add all the holy basil leaves at once and fold them through the rice with 4–5 broad strokes of the spatula. The residual heat of the rice and wok will wilt the basil in 20–30 seconds — you want it collapsed and glossy but not black or slimy. Holy basil wilts much faster than Italian basil and turns bitter if overcooked. The leaves should turn a deep, jewel-like green and release a wave of clove-anise fragrance. Taste and adjust with a few drops more fish sauce if needed.

In a small wok or skillet, heat the remaining 10 g of oil over high heat until it shimmers and just begins to smoke. Crack eggs into the oil and let them fry undisturbed for 60–90 seconds. The whites should blister and puff immediately on contact, forming golden lacey edges while the yolk stays barely set and glossy. Tilt the pan and baste the yolk with hot oil using a spoon. The egg is done when the white is fully set and golden-fringed, the yolk still deep orange and runny. Serve immediately atop the rice.

name: Pad Kra Pao
description: Ground pork stir-fried over violent heat with bird's eye chilies and Thai holy basil until the meat caramelizes at the edges and the whole dish blooms with a peppery, clove-like fragrance that holy basil alone produces — a Bangkok street-food staple that takes 8 minutes, demands ferocious heat, and rewards with an intensity that formal restaurant versions rarely match.
ingredients: 1¾ cups ground pork, or coarsely hand-chopped pork (400 g)
1 tablespoon soy sauce, thin, not dark
1 teaspoon oyster-flavored sugar, or palm sugar
1 cup Thai holy basil, loosely packed; leaves only; kra pao
2 fried egg, one per servings, kai dao
steps: Combine oyster sauce, fish sauce, soy sauce, and sugar in a small bowl. Stir until the sugar dissolves. Taste and adjust: it should be intensely savory, salty, slightly sweet, and smell powerfully of fermented seafood and caramel. Set beside the stove. In pad kra pao, there is no time for measuring once the wok is hot — everything must be ready before you start.

Heat a wok or large cast-iron pan over the highest possible heat until it begins to smoke. Add the oil and heat for 15 seconds. Add the chilies and garlic simultaneously. Stir-fry, keeping everything moving, for 30-45 seconds. The garlic should be fragrant and just beginning to color at the edges — not burnt. The chilies will release intense capsaicin vapor; ensure ventilation. This step is fast and violent.

Add the ground pork to the wok in one addition. Press it flat against the hot surface and let it sear without stirring for 30-45 seconds until the contact side turns grey-to-caramelized. Then break it up and stir-fry vigorously for 2-3 minutes, pressing and breaking apart any clumps. Pour in the pre-mixed sauce and the water. Continue stir-frying over maximum heat for another minute until the sauce has reduced and coated every piece of meat in a sticky, dark glaze. The pan should sound like it is sizzling furiously — not steaming.

Remove the wok from heat. Add all the holy basil leaves at once and toss rapidly — residual heat will wilt the basil in 15-20 seconds. Holy basil releases its best aroma when it hits heat but is not overcooked: the leaves should be wilted but still intensely fragrant and not uniformly black. Serve immediately over jasmine rice, topped with a fried egg cooked in very hot oil until the edges are crispy and lacy.

name: Thai Fish Cakes (Tod Mun Pla)
description: Bouncy, herb-charged fish cakes kneaded until springy, fried in oil until golden — the protein energy of fish, lifted with kaffir lime leaf and fiery red curry paste.
ingredients: 3 white fish, pin-boned fillets, tilapia, Spanish mackerel, or snapper (400 g)
2 tablespoons Thai red curry paste (30 g)
8 kaffir lime leaves, central stem removeds, finely chiffonade
⅔ cup long beans or green beans, cut into 3 mm rounds (60 g)
steps: Cut the fish into rough chunks. Pulse in a food processor until the fish breaks down into a coarse paste — approximately 15–20 short pulses. Do not blend to a smooth puree; you want some texture remaining. Add the curry paste, fish sauce, egg, and cornstarch. Pulse 10 more times to combine. Then switch from pulsing to processing: run continuously for 30–45 seconds. The mixture will visibly change — it begins to gather into itself, pulling away from the bowl sides and becoming sticky and elastic. This is the myosin protein network forming, the same mechanism that makes bouncy fish balls. This step is not optional.

Transfer the fish paste to a bowl. Add the kaffir lime leaf chiffonade and sliced beans. Fold in firmly with a spatula — not gently, but with real pressure to distribute the additions without breaking the protein network already developed. At this stage, many Thai cooks slap the mixture against the bowl 10–15 times: lift and throw the paste back into the bowl to drive out air bubbles and further tighten the network. Refrigerate the paste for 15 minutes — chilling makes shaping much easier.

Heat the oil in a wok or deep pan to 175°C (350°F). Wet your palms with cold water. Scoop 2 heaped tablespoons of paste and form into a flat disc 1.5 cm thick and 7 cm diameter — they should look like hockey pucks, not balls. Slide gently into the oil. Fry 4–5 at a time without crowding. Cook 2–3 minutes per side until deep golden-brown all over. The cakes will float and puff slightly as they cook — a good sign. Test one by cutting in half: it should be cooked through with no translucent center and a dense, bouncy interior texture.

Drain on paper towels for 60 seconds only — too long and they cool and lose their crackle. Arrange on a serving plate. Serve immediately with Thai cucumber relish (ajat): thin-sliced cucumber and shallot in sweet vinegar with crushed peanuts and coriander. The cool, sharp relish is not optional accompaniment — it is the counterpoint the richness demands.

name: Thai Larb Gai
description: Quick-cooked minced chicken tossed with toasted rice powder, lime, fish sauce, and an avalanche of fresh herbs — bright, sharp, and texturally alive.
ingredients: 1¾ cups ground chicken, or hand-minced thigh meat (400 g)
2½ tablespoons raw glutinous rice, uncooked; sticky (30 g)
2 teaspoons dried chili flakes, or to taste, prik bon
2 shallots, thinly sliced into rings (60 g)
A handful of fresh mint leaves, torn (20 g)
A handful of fresh cilantro, roughly chopped
¾ lemongrass, tender inner stalk only, minced
steps: Place the raw glutinous rice in a dry wok or heavy skillet over medium heat. Toast, stirring constantly, for 5–8 minutes until each grain turns golden-brown and the kitchen fills with a popcorn-like, nutty fragrance. Do not walk away — the transition from golden to burnt takes seconds. Transfer to a mortar or spice grinder and grind to a coarse powder (the texture of fine breadcrumbs). This powder is the secret texture of larb: it absorbs the dressing and gives the dish its characteristic sandy bite.

Heat a wok over high heat until smoking. Add the ground chicken with no oil — the natural fat in the meat is sufficient and oil would cause steaming. Break the meat apart rapidly with a spatula, spreading it thin across the hot wok surface. Cook until just no longer pink, about 3–4 minutes. Do not cook through completely — the residual heat and lime acid will finish it. The goal is barely cooked, still juicy chicken.

Working while the chicken is still very hot (the heat helps the dressing penetrate), add fish sauce, lime juice, dried chili flakes, and sugar. Toss vigorously. Taste immediately — the balance is the dish. It should hit sour first, then salty, then heat building at the back of the throat. Adjust: more lime for brightness, more fish sauce for depth, more chili for fire.

Fold in the shallots, mint, cilantro, scallion, and minced lemongrass. Scatter the toasted rice powder over the top and fold in gently — you want it distributed but not completely buried. Taste one final time. Serve immediately on a plate lined with cabbage leaves, with extra mint and raw vegetables on the side. Larb deteriorates quickly as the herbs wilt and the rice powder hydrates — this is a dish that lives in the moment.

name: Toasted Farro Salad with Roasted Vegetables
description: Whole farro toasted in a dry pan until nutty and golden, then simmered until pleasantly chewy — tossed warm with caramelized roasted vegetables, fresh herbs, lemon, and good olive oil in the manner of Tuscan cucina povera: simply excellent ingredients treated with respect.
ingredients: 1½ cups whole farro, not pearled (300 g)
3¾ cups water or vegetable stock (900 g)
1½ zucchinis, cut into 2 cm pieces (250 g)
1 red onion, cut into wedges (150 g)
Half an eggplant, cut into 2 cm cubes (200 g)
⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided (80 g)
A handful of fresh flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped (20 g)
A small handful of fresh mint leaves, torn
⅓ cup toasted pine nuts or walnuts (40 g)
steps: Place the farro in a large dry skillet over medium heat. Toast, stirring constantly, for 4–6 minutes until the grains smell nutty and are golden — some grains may lightly pop. This step is optional but transforms the flavor dramatically. The toasted grains will have a nuttier, more complex flavor after cooking.

Transfer toasted farro to a pot. Cover with generously salted water or stock (3 parts liquid to 1 part farro by volume). Bring to a boil, reduce to a steady simmer, and cook uncovered for 30–40 minutes for whole farro (20–25 for semi-pearled) until the grains are tender but still have a distinct chew — al dente, like a well-cooked barley. Drain any excess liquid.

Toss all the vegetables with a generous amount of olive oil, salt, and chili flakes on a large sheet pan. Spread in a single layer — do not crowd or they will steam. Roast at 220 C (425 F) for 25–30 minutes, turning once halfway, until caramelized and charred at the edges — particularly the cherry tomatoes, which should burst and concentrate.

While both the farro and vegetables are still warm, combine them in a large bowl. Drizzle with remaining olive oil and lemon juice. Add lemon zest, chili flakes, parsley, mint, and toasted nuts. Toss together gently — you want the warm farro to absorb the lemon and oil. Taste and adjust salt, acid, and oil. The salad is excellent warm, but also very good at room temperature.

name: Turkish Çılbır
description: Poached eggs draped over cold garlicked yogurt and drowned in sizzling Aleppo-red butter — a 15th-century Ottoman dish that turns breakfast into theatre with its collision of cool, hot, bright, and smoky.
ingredients: ¾ cup full-fat Greek yogurt, room temperature (200 g)
1 garlic clove, minced to a paste
1 tablespoon white wine vinegar, for poaching water
steps: Mince the garlic to a smooth paste with the flat of a knife and a pinch of salt — chop, then smear and drag the blade repeatedly until no chunks remain. Stir it into the yogurt with the remaining salt. Beat until completely smooth. The yogurt must be at room temperature before serving — cold yogurt on hot eggs creates an unpleasant thermal shock and mutes the garlic. Spread it onto the plate now and let it temper while you poach the eggs.

Fill a wide saucepan with at least 8 cm of water. Add the white wine vinegar — the acid tightens the egg white around the yolk. Bring to just below a simmer: small bubbles rising from the bottom, surface barely trembling at 80–85°C. Crack each egg individually into a small cup. Create a gentle whirlpool in the water with a spoon. Slide one egg into the center of the whirlpool; the rotation wraps the white around the yolk. Cook 3–3.5 minutes for a runny yolk. Remove with a slotted spoon, blot the underside on a folded cloth, and place directly onto the yogurt.

In a small saucepan or butter warmer, melt the butter over medium heat until it foams. The moment the foam subsides and the butter turns a deep golden amber, remove from heat and immediately add the Aleppo pepper — it will sizzle and bloom in the hot fat. Swirl the pan. Work fast: the residual heat continues cooking the butter, and Aleppo scorches quickly. The butter should turn a vivid red-orange and smell smoky, sweet, and fragrant.

The eggs are already on the yogurt. Pour the sizzling Aleppo butter directly over the eggs and yogurt — it will pool and seep into the white yogurt, creating rivers of deep red. Scatter fresh dill fronds over everything. Serve immediately with warm flatbread or crusty white bread on the side for scooping. The temperature contrast is the whole point: cold yogurt beneath, hot egg above, sizzling butter cascading over.

name: Turkish Roasted Vegetables with Pomegranate
description: Roasted zucchini, eggplant, and red pepper dressed with pomegranate molasses and fresh herbs — caramelized edges, sweet-tart dressing, and the tang of yogurt beneath.
ingredients: 1½ zucchinis, cut into 3 cm cubes; courgette (300 g)
¾ globe eggplant, cut into 3 cm cubes (300 g)
1 red bell pepper, cut into 3 cm strips (200 g)
1 red onion, cut into wedges (150 g)
A handful of fresh mint leaves, torn
A handful of flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped
¾ cup Turkish-style thick yogurt, süzme yoğurt (200 g)
steps: Preheat oven to 220°C (430°F) with a large sheet tray inside. Toss all cut vegetables and the unpeeled garlic cloves with the olive oil and salt in a large bowl. Spread in a single layer on the hot tray — crowding causes steaming. Roast for 25–30 minutes, turning once halfway, until the edges are deeply caramelized and the zucchini and eggplant have collapsed and charred in patches.

While the vegetables are still warm, squeeze the roasted garlic from their skins directly over the vegetables and stir gently to break them into the mix. Drizzle the pomegranate molasses over and sprinkle the sumac. Toss gently to coat without breaking up the vegetables further. Scatter the fresh mint and parsley. Taste for salt and acidity — the dressing should be assertively tart.

Spread the cold yogurt in a generous layer on the base of a wide serving plate, creating a swoosh with the back of a spoon. Pile the warm dressed vegetables directly onto the yogurt. The contrast of cold, tangy yogurt and warm, sweet-tart vegetables is the heart of the dish. Serve immediately.

name: Vietnamese Caramel Fish (Cá Kho Tộ)
description: Catfish braised in a Vietnamese caramel of burnished sugar and fish sauce in a clay pot until the sauce reduces to a sticky, lacquered glaze and the fish falls into sweet-salty, deeply savory flakes.
ingredients: 3 catfish steaks, 3cm thicks, cá tra (600 g)
⅓ cup granulated sugar, for caramel (60 g)
½ cup young coconut water, or water (120 ml)
A knob of fresh ginger, thin coins
steps: In a clay pot or small heavy saucepan over medium heat, add the sugar in an even layer without stirring. Watch as the sugar at the edges begins to melt and turn amber (about 3 minutes). Only then tilt the pan gently to encourage even melting — do not stir with a spoon or it will crystallize. Cook until the caramel is a deep mahogany-brown (not black) and smells of bitter toffee. This is the defining flavor of kho tộ — a dark, slightly bitter caramel that balances the salty fish sauce.

Pour the fish sauce into the hot caramel (spatter warning!). Add the coconut water and stir — the mixture will bubble intensely and the caramel will seize before re-dissolving. Add the shallots, garlic, ginger, chili, and black pepper. Lay the catfish steaks in the pot in a single layer, spooning the caramel sauce over. Cover and braise over medium-low heat for 15 minutes, turning the fish once at the 8-minute mark.

Uncover the pot and increase heat to medium-high. Simmer the sauce, basting the fish continuously with a spoon, for 5–8 minutes until the sauce has reduced to a thick, dark, syrupy glaze that coats every surface of the fish. The pot will begin to sizzle more intensely as the water evaporates. Remove from heat. Scatter green onion over the top. Serve directly from the clay pot with steamed jasmine rice.

name: Thit Kho To (Vietnamese Caramel Pork)
description: Pork belly braised in a dark amber caramel, fish sauce, and fresh coconut water until the fat is translucent-soft and the meat drinks in the salty-sweet glaze — the quintessential dish of Southern Vietnamese home cooking.
ingredients: 800 g pork belly, skin-on, cut into 4 cm pieces
¼ cup fish sauce, nuoc mam (60 g)
⅓ cup granulated white sugar, for caramel (80 g)
1½ tablespoons palm sugar or brown sugar (20 g)
Half a Thai bird's eye chili, sliced; optional
steps: Place a clay pot or heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the white sugar in a thin, even layer. Watch carefully without stirring — as the edges begin to melt and turn amber (about 4–5 minutes), tilt the pan to distribute. When the sugar is fully liquid and the color of dark mahogany, with thin wisps of smoke just beginning, remove from heat immediately.

Add the pork belly pieces to the hot caramel and stir quickly to coat. Stand back — the fat will cause violent sputtering. Sear the pork in the caramel for 3–4 minutes, turning with tongs, until each piece is coated in the dark caramel and beginning to brown.

Add shallots and garlic to the pot and stir for 1 minute. Pour in coconut water and fish sauce — the liquid will seize and splatter as it hits the caramel, then rapidly dissolve it. Add palm sugar and black pepper. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, then reduce to the lowest possible simmer. Cover and cook for 45 minutes.

After 45 minutes, add the peeled hard-boiled eggs. Gently turn them to coat in the broth. Cook uncovered for another 20–25 minutes, occasionally spooning broth over the pork, until the broth has reduced to a glossy, syrupy sauce and the fat on the pork is completely tender and translucent.
Ladle pork, eggs, and sauce into bowls or onto a platter. Scatter green onions and optional chili over the top. Serve immediately with steamed jasmine rice and pickled daikon.

name: Bun Cha Meatballs
description: Hanoi's answer to the grill: fat-streaked pork patties charred over coal until they blister and caramelize at the edges, then plunged into a cool, sweet-sour nuoc cham that tempers the smoke and draws out the meat's depth. The char is not incidental — it is the recipe.
ingredients: ½ teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground
¾ cup warm water, for dipping broth
3 tablespoons fish sauce, for dipping broth
2 garlic cloves, thinly sliced; for broth
1 small red chili, thinly sliced; for broth
steps: Combine ground pork, minced shallots, garlic, fish sauce, sugar, and pepper in a large bowl. Mix with your hands for 2-3 minutes using a squeezing, folding motion — not stirring. The mixture should become slightly sticky and cohesive. The fat should begin to emulsify with the lean meat. Refrigerate for 30 minutes to firm.

Dissolve sugar in warm water. Add fish sauce, lime juice, sliced garlic, and chili. Stir and taste — the broth should land in four-part harmony: salty, sweet, sour, and funky, with no single note dominating. This is the dipping broth that the cooked patties will rest in, so it needs to be slightly more intense than you would drink — the meat will dilute it.

Form the chilled pork into flat, palm-sized patties about 3/4 inch thick (or small round meatballs for bun cha proper). Grill over high charcoal heat or a screaming hot cast-iron grill pan. Cook 3-4 minutes per side without moving — you want aggressive charring, not steaming. The fat will drip, flare, and add smoke flavor. Authentic bun cha has black char marks and a caramelized exterior.

Transfer the hot grilled patties directly into the bowls of nuoc cham broth. Serve with a plate of fresh herbs, vermicelli noodles on the side, and extra chili. The patties will continue steaming in the broth, picking up the sour-sweet nuoc cham and tempering the smoke. This is meant to be eaten immediately, scooping noodles into the broth bowl at the table.

name: Yangzhou Fried Rice
description: The most celebrated Chinese fried rice — day-old jasmine cooked over a blistering wok until each grain is separate and kissed with wok hei, bound with egg in two stages, studded with sweet shrimp, smoky char siu, peas and scallion. Prestige in a bowl.
ingredients: 3¼ cups day-old cooked jasmine rice, cold (600 g)
1 cup medium shrimp, peeled and deveined (150 g)
100 g char siu or honey-glazed ham, diced
½ cup frozen peas, thawed (80 g)
3 tablespoons neutral oil, vegetable or peanut (45 ml)
steps: This dish cooks in under 5 minutes once the wok is hot — everything must be ready before you touch the heat. Break up the cold rice with your hands, rubbing any clumps between your palms until every grain is separate and dry — clumped rice steams instead of frying. Beat the eggs lightly with a fork and a pinch of salt. Pat the shrimp dry with paper towels. Dice the char siu or ham into 1cm cubes. Have the sauces measured and combined in a small bowl. Slice the scallions with white and green parts kept separate. Line all components up beside the wok in the order they will be added.

Heat a wok or very large, heavy skillet over the highest possible heat for 2 full minutes — it should be smoking before any oil goes in. Add 2 tablespoons of the oil and immediately add the shrimp in a single layer. Sear without stirring for 45 seconds until pink and curled, then toss and cook 30 seconds more. Remove from the wok immediately. Add the diced char siu for 30 seconds just to warm and slightly caramelize the edges. Remove and set aside with the shrimp.

With the wok still blazing hot, add the remaining oil and swirl to coat. Pour the beaten eggs into the center of the wok — they will set almost instantly. Scramble them very briefly, just until they are 70% set but still wet and glossy. Immediately add the cold rice on top of the wet egg, pressing it down into the egg. Toss vigorously — every 30 seconds pause to let the rice sit against the hot wok, then toss again. This alternation between contact and toss is what creates wok hei, the smoky 'breath of the wok.' Cook for 3–4 minutes total.

Pour the combined soy sauce and oyster sauce over the rice and toss immediately and vigorously — the sauces evaporate quickly over high heat and should perfume rather than wet the rice. Add the peas and the white scallion parts, toss 30 seconds. Return the shrimp and char siu and toss just to incorporate and warm through. Finish with white pepper and a drizzle of sesame oil off the heat — sesame oil added to a hot wok becomes bitter. Scatter the green scallion tops over the top. Serve immediately — fried rice waits for no one.
